As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.

paper.title: Viscoelastic behavior at high volume fraction of magnetorheological suspensions in the presence of discontinuous shear thickening
paper.summary: This paper presents a study of the viscoelastic behavior of suspensions of carbonyl iron particles coated with a superplastifier molecule and dispersed in ethylene glycol. The experiments were done in plate-plate configuration with the rheometer MCR502 of Anton Paar. The discontinuous shear thickening (DST) transition manifests by a large jump of the storage and loss modulus. For low magnetic fields ( H <___50___kA/m) the increase of moduli is at least of two orders of magnitude compared to the one induced by the magnetic field in the absence of DST. The behavior of the critical strain and the critical stress where the transition happens are presented for different frequencies and fields and a qualitative interpretation of the observed behavior is presented.

paper.title: Ultraviolet Raman spectroscopy using multimode aluminum oxide waveguides
paper.summary: Waveguide-based Raman spectroscopy offers a route toward compact and integrated photonic sensors. While most waveguide Raman platforms operate in the near-infrared, extending excitation toward the visible and ultraviolet is attractive because shorter excitation wavelengths can provide substantially stronger Raman scattering and access to resonance-enhanced molecular responses. This transition, however, places greater demands on the photonic material because of optical loss, absorption and waveguide-generated spectral background. Here, we investigate aluminum oxide ($Al_2O_3$) waveguides as a low-background platform for Raman spectroscopy at 532 nm and 325 nm using a back-collected excitation and detection geometry. At 532 nm, after normalization to the incident excitation power-time product, the measured $Al_2O_3$ background was more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of $Si_3N_4$. Under 325 nm excitation, the waveguides maintained a weak and reproducible spectral background across the investigated widths. Using immersion oil as a model analyte deposited over the waveguide surface, we demonstrate that analyte-specific Raman fingerprints can be recovered above the waveguide background at both wavelengths. Signal-to-background ratio and spectral contrast were used to quantify analyte visibility relative to the waveguide background, and both metrics consistently confirmed clear detection of the analyte bands. These results demonstrate that $Al_2O_3$ combines low measured spectral background with operation from the visible into the ultraviolet, providing a promising route toward integrated Raman spectroscopy at shorter excitation wavelengths.

paper.title: An approximate separation of the electron and positron degrees of freedom in the Dirac-Heisenberg-Wigner formalism
paper.summary: Here we study the quantum relativistic phase-space description of the Dirac field referred to as the Dirac--Heisenberg--Wigner (DHW) formalism. By applying a systematic expansion procedure in weak electromagnetic fields (compared to the Schwinger critical field) and slow temporal and long spatial scales (compared to the Compton scales), the 16 scalar phase-space functions of the DHW equations can be reduced to 8 scalars. By making a further change of variables, the equations can be interpreted as four evolution equations for the electron degrees of freedom and four for the positron degrees of freedom. We refer to these equations as the weakly coupled electron-positron (WCEP) limit of the DHW equations. Unlike the case after a Foldy--Wouthuysen transformation has been made, the electron and positron degrees of freedom remain weakly coupled. Naturally, further approximations can be made on the 4+4 equations so that only 4 equations for one particle species remain. Importantly, the expansion scheme can be carried out to all orders, in which case the reduced 4+4 model, contrary to other reduced models, will cover most quantum relativistic effects. Specifically, this includes vacuum polarization, a phenomenon that otherwise has been added phenomenologically, but here appears naturally as a feature of the general expansion scheme.

paper.title: FLUCS: a modular GPU-native framework for fluid and plasma turbulence
paper.summary: We present FLUCS, an open-source framework for solving systems of partial differential equations efficiently on graphics processing units (GPUs), targeting models of fluid and plasma turbulence. It comprises a set of numerical solvers specialised for a well-defined class of problems and independently developed systems that supply specific systems of equations. This allows different models to share numerical infrastructure while retaining control over their individual implementation and optimisation. The present release provides a Fourier pseudospectral solver for one-, two-, and three-dimensional periodic domains solved on a single NVIDIA GPU, with integrating-factor time integration and several time-stepping and dealiasing methods. We verify its convergence, quantify its computational costs, and demonstrate its application to three reduced models of fusion and astrophysical plasma turbulence.

paper.title: Hydrodynamic regimes of the edge-tone in a simplified recorder mouthpiece
paper.summary: The acoustic mechanism of flue instruments originates in the interaction of an air jet with a sharp edge, the labium. Previous studies have examined isolated edge-tones or full instruments in which acoustic resonance obscures the underlying hydrodynamics, and a systematic understanding of how geometric parameters govern jet stability is lacking. We present a large-scale parametric study of the jet-labium interaction in a simplified recorder mouthpiece without a resonator, using more than 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations with an immersed boundary method. We vary the mouth distance, the labium angle, the vertical offset of the labium, and the Reynolds number (Re), and characterize the dynamics through spectra of the transverse force on the labium. The baseline configuration oscillates as a predominantly periodic Stage I edge-tone with Strouhal number St ~ 0.07, nearly constant for Re >= 330 and for all labium angles at the baseline mouth distance, so the frequency is set by the geometry rather than by viscosity. The mouth distance has the strongest influence: it is the only parameter that introduces a second oscillation stage, and the Stage I frequency is inversely proportional to it. The second stage is weakly present at five and six windway heights, established from six and a half, and dominant from eight, where it strongly modulates the amplitude. The vertical offset mainly affects the strength of the oscillation, and the labium angle does not change the instability mechanism. A baseline configuration is identified for future aeroacoustic coupling studies.

paper.title: Reconfigurable Generation of Terahertz Spiral Vector Beams Based on All-Dielectric Cascaded Metasurfaces
paper.summary: The reconfigurable generation of complex structured terahertz (THz) fields, and vector beams in particular, remains a significant challenge. Here, we propose a novel all-dielectric cascaded-metasurface scheme for the reconfigurable generation of THz spiral vector beams. By combining an isotropic phase-compensation layer with an anisotropic circular-polarization-sensitive layer, together with a new phase design tailored to spiral beams, we achieve independent control of the left- and right-handed circularly polarized (LCP and RCP) components through the relative rotation angle between the two layers. Under linearly polarized THz wave illumination, THz vector beams with switchable spiral numbers of 1-3 and reversible circular-polarization handedness are demonstrated at frequencies around 0.9 THz. Moreover, owing to the longitudinal evolution characteristic of spiral beams, the three generated THz vector beams exhibit azimuthal rotations of 279.9°, 125.7° and 75.5°, respectively, along the propagation direction. Such complex THz vector beams, which combine reconfigurability with longitudinal evolution, are expected to find applications in emerging fields such as next-generation wireless communications and THz imaging. The proposed generation scheme also offers a useful reference for the reconfigurable generation of high-dimensional vector beams.

paper.title: Accelerating Computation and Resolving Extraneous Roots in the Kinetic Plasma Dispersion Relation Solver BO
paper.summary: Kinetic dispersion relations are widely used to study waves and instabilities in space, astrophysical, and laboratory plasmas. Iterative root searches depend on initial guesses and may fail to converge or miss important branches. The BO/PDRK solvers [Comput. Phys. Commun. 244, 343-371 (2019)] use rational pole expansions to transform the nonlinear dispersion relation into a matrix eigenvalue problem, obtaining all roots of the approximated relation in one calculation. However, high cyclotron harmonics enlarge the matrix and slow computation, while extraneous roots are difficult to separate from physical modes. We develop BO-T (BO-Tian), an improved version of BO combining two methods. First, for matrix reduction, BO-T applies rank factorization to combined residue matrices, preserving the rational dispersion relation and accounting for the removed pole eigenvalues. Second, for root screening, BO-T uses contour comparison between approximate and reference kinetic dispersion matrices along a closed contour enclosing no poles. This provides a sufficient condition for preserving local root counts, with error bounds for isolated roots and criteria for growth rate signs. Benchmarks on representative electrostatic and electromagnetic cases show speedups of about 10 to 140 for matrix assembly and eigenvalue calculation, exceeding 30 in most cases with high cyclotron harmonics. Root screening recovers the main unstable branches in agreement with published and archived dispersion curves.

paper.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
paper.summary: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

paper.title: Non-Hermitian Spectral Topology Shaped by Memory
paper.summary: Non-Hermitian spectral topology has transformed our understanding of bulk--boundary correspondence in open systems, yet its exploration has largely remained within the Markovian regime of instantaneous coupling. Here, we reveal how memory shapes non-Hermitian spectral topology by extending coupling asymmetry from space to time. Spatiotemporal nonreciprocity and memory-induced spectral multivaluedness give rise to nontrivial spectral topology on multi-sheeted Riemann surfaces, governed by both spatial connectivity and interaction history. Coherent interference among long-range memory channels can induce anomalous spectral winding and skin localization opposite to the dominant-coupling direction. Moreover, asymmetric retardation alone can generate non-Hermitian spectral topology and skin accumulation even in the absence of spatial coupling asymmetry. Channel dissipation further drives topological transitions that reverse the skin effect, with a critical point at matched channel and lattice decay rates. We validate the anomalous skin effect and its dissipation-controlled reversal through full-wave simulations and microwave experiments. Our results establish time nonlocality as a fundamental degree of freedom in non-Hermitian topology, revealing phenomena inaccessible within the Markovian paradigm.

paper.title: Plasmoid Instability in Inhomogeneous Current Sheets
paper.summary: Plasmoid instability in inhomogeneous current sheets is investigated using electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulations of collisionless magnetic reconnection. Simulations with and without small random perturbations are compared to examine the effects of symmetry breaking and spatial inhomogeneity. The current-sheet width immediately before disruption remains close to the electron skin depth, whereas the disruption aspect ratio varies significantly between primary and later current sheets. Random perturbations also produce asymmetric plasmoid topologies in which neighboring X points no longer share a common separatrix. These results suggest that spatial inhomogeneity is an important factor in the disruption of dynamically evolving current sheets.

paper.title: A Large Eddy Simulation Study of Turbine Pitch Motion Effects on Power Generation in Fully Developed Floating Wind Turbine Arrays
paper.summary: Interactions between floating wind turbines and the marine atmospheric boundary layer affect turbine wakes and power output. This study examines the impact of turbine representations and platform pitching motion on power predictions for aligned floating wind turbine arrays. Large-eddy simulations (LES) are performed for a fully developed wind turbine array boundary layer with periodic streamwise and spanwise boundary conditions and moving surface drag (MOSD) at the bottom surface. A proposed power-curve-aware extension of the conventional actuator disk model (PCADM) is compared with the traditional constant coefficient actuator disk model (CCADM), which is valid in principle only during Region 2 operation. Harmonic pitching motion matched to a representative ocean wave frequency is prescribed for IEA 15MW turbines mounted on the UMaine VolturnUS-S platform. Results demonstrate that the CCADM produces unphysical power overshoot when relative velocities induced by harmonic pitching periodically exceed rated speed, while the PCADM eliminates these unrealistic excursions from the actual turbine operating range. Various wind-wave conditions and relative pitching motions for an aligned farm with PCADM turbines are analyzed, including in-phase, opposite-phase, and incommensurate-phase row-to-row relative turbine motion. Results reveal that, depending on operational regions, turbine pitching motion can either increase or decrease mean turbine power output. Among the relative phases considered, in-phase motions produce larger fluctuations at the farm scale due to stronger turbine-turbine correlations. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for turbine motion and associated changes in operational regions when modeling turbine and wind farm power production in LES of offshore floating wind farms using actuator disk representations.

paper.title: Dual-rate optical frequency comb based on a cylindrical microresonator with a nanoscale radius variation
paper.summary: We theoretically find that a cylindrical microresonator with nanoscale radius variation can be a source of coherent microcombs with two repetition rates, independently controlled by the device geometry. This phenomenon arises from the formation of two-dimensional axial-azimuthal dissipative Kerr solitons (2D DKS), which we discovered through numerical simulations of the nonlinearly coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with realistic microresonator device parameters. We demonstrate that, despite the variation in the dispersion characteristics of azimuthal modes at different axial numbers, the spontaneous synchronization mechanism leads to a unified soliton repetition rate. We consider near-parabolic variations in the radius of a cylindrical resonator, compatible with the surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) platform. In our example, we generate 2D DKS with an azimuthal rate of approximately 329 GHz and an axial rate of 6 GHz, which can be adjusted on demand by selecting the appropriate resonator geometry, thereby promising compact sources of frequency combs operating simultaneously across different frequency scales.

paper.title: Teacher-guided multi-task learning for integrated plasma monitoring on EAST
paper.summary: This paper integrates tokamak plasma disruption prediction, Edge-Localized Mode (ELM) monitoring, Multifaceted Asymmetric Radiation From the Edge (MARFE) detection, and H/L-mode identification into a unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL) model. This integration aims to realize MTL's potential for improving task performance while reducing inference time. However, on datasets constructed from selected EAST discharges recorded between 2015 and 2020, this study found that the traditional MTL method underperformed the corresponding Single-Task Learning (STL) method on some tasks. This performance degradation is the well-known issue of negative transfer. To address this issue, this study proposes the teacher-guided MTL method, using task-specific STL ensembles (teachers) to guide the training of an MTL model (student). The ensemble teachers guide training through soft-target distillation losses for each task of the MTL student model, and increased weighting of each shot's peak-disruptivity window in the disruption prediction label-supervised loss. Test-set results showed that the teacher-guided MTL method outperformed the corresponding STL method in ROC-AUC for all four tasks, eliminating the negative transfer observed with the traditional MTL method. In addition, on the same single GPU or single physical CPU core, the MTL student model can substantially reduce the inference time required to generate all four task outputs compared with the four STL baseline models. This paper offers a promising route to plasma monitoring systems that cover a broader range of phenomena, improve per-task performance and reduce inference time with limited real-time computational resources, supporting future high-performance plasma operation.

paper.title: An analytical framework for wave-coherent airflow over fast surface waves
paper.summary: Classical theories attribute wind-wave momentum transfer to a critical layer, where the mean wind speed equals the wave phase speed. For waves that travel faster than the near-surface wind, this layer may lie outside the wave boundary layer or be absent altogether. We develop an analytical description of the wave-coherent airflow in this regime for a prescribed mean wind, using a Wentzel--Kramers--Brillouin--Jeffreys (WKBJ) approximation to the viscous Orr--Sommerfeld equation in wave-following coordinates. The solution combines an outer Rayleigh mode, which carries the dominant wave-coherent motion, with a thin viscous Stokes layer that supplies the phase shift producing the pressure form stress. At leading order, the form stress scales with the inverse square root of the wave Reynolds number, with a coefficient set by an integral of the outer response, and transfers momentum from the waves to the air. For an exponential mean profile, the WKBJ approximation gives closed-form expressions for the wave-coherent response. To accommodate the rapid near-surface variation of realistic wall-bounded profiles, we develop a long-wave expansion near the surface and match it to the outer WKBJ mode (LW--WKBJ). For wall-modelled simulations, whose first resolved level lies above the viscous sublayer, we replace the molecular viscosity in the Stokes layer with a constant-stress effective viscosity. Using mean profiles from direct numerical simulations and wave-phase-resolved large-eddy simulations, the LW--WKBJ framework closely reproduces the dominant wave-coherent velocity and pressure obtained from numerical solutions and available simulation data. The predicted form-stress coefficients also agree well with the available LES estimates.

paper.title: Non-contact temperature sensing and optical scatter in cryogenically-cooled crystalline silicon
paper.summary: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of $(4.43\pm0.2)\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{sr^{-1}}$ at a scattering angle of $θ_{s} = 7.5^\circ$ over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.

paper.title: Equipartition between Alfvénic turbulence and energetic ions as the origin of the -5 common spectrum in the heliosphere
paper.summary: Suprathermal ion tails throughout the heliosphere follow a ``common spectrum,'' $f(v)\propto v^{-5}$. We show that scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfvénic turbulence and the ions it accelerates predicts both this exponent and the absolute amplitude, $F(v)=B^2/(16π^3 m_i v^5)$, with no free parameters. The prediction agrees within a factor of a few with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra across three decades in magnetic energy. We argue that this saturated level is reached where strong turbulence accelerates particles locally; quiet-time tails lie well below it, consistent with nonlocal acceleration.

paper.title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
paper.summary: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

paper.title: Intensity-Domain Demultiplexing of Orbital Angular Momentum Channels for Optical Communication
paper.summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements that separate the channels at the receiver side. Here we adopt the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis, which makes the receiver the optical counterpart of the circular antenna arrays used in radio OAM links: the petal pattern of topological charge $\ell$ carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order $2\ell$, so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel, without gratings or mode sorters. The petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization. A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array reaches 5.2 Gb/s below the forward error correction threshold, 2.6 Gb/s per channel from a 1.4 GHz photoreceiver.

paper.title: Stress-enhanced diffusion in Yukawa crystals
paper.summary: Self-diffusion in crystallized Coulomb (Yukawa) plasmas proceeds by the thermally activated formation of vacancy-interstitial pairs and the migration of these defects through the lattice, commonly known as Frenkel pairs in the materials literature. Molecular dynamics has recently resolved an Eyring law for diffusion in unstrained crystals, which we generalize to deformed crystals in this work. We simulate sheared Yukawa crystals and show that a static elastic strain exponentially enhances diffusion due to the additional elastic energy stored in the region that participates in Frenkel pair formation relative to the unstrained crystal: $D(\varepsilon)=D_0(Γ^{*})\exp[V^{*}σ/k_{\rm B}T]$, with $σ=\tfrac12μ\varepsilon^{2}$ the elastic energy density stored by the shear strain $\varepsilon$ and $V^{*}$ the activation volume. We find a single activation volume $N_{\rm act} = n_iV^{*}\simeq31$ suffices for typical astrophysical screenings with a reduction at higher screening. This suggests Frenkel pair formation requires only a brief coordination of the nearest neighbors at a thermal maximum in oscillation. Stress-enhanced diffusion supplies a microphysical mechanism for creep in strained neutron star crusts and crystallizing white dwarf cores.

paper.title: As a matter of reconstruction -- varying the magnetic Prandtl number in implicit large eddy simulations
paper.summary: The magnetic Prandtl number ($\mathrm{Pm}$), the ratio of viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, spans many orders of magnitude in astrophysical plasmas. It shapes how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In direct numerical simulations (DNS) the viscosity and magnetic diffusivity can be controlled explicitly and independently, whereas in implicit large eddy simulations (ILES) they are set by the numerical scheme. We test whether, in a finite-volume code, $\mathrm{Pm}$ can be varied through the reconstruction scheme by applying different methods to the hydro and magnetic variables. As a proof of concept, we simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. We measure the effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales. Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective magnetic Prandtl number and vice versa. We demonstrate that a mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone results in a $\gtrsim20\times$ change in $\mathrm{Pm}$. A comparison of DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES. Mixed reconstruction thus offers a simple and efficient way to explore $\mathrm{Pm} \not\simeq 1$ in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

paper.title: From proof of concept to practice: the next decade of artificial intelligence in metasurface photonics
paper.summary: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence has learned to predict electromagnetic responses rapidly and generate high-performance metasurface designs. However, one question remains open: compared with conventional design workflows that contain no learned model, has it made the complete design workflow faster, and are the resulting devices better? We argue that the answer depends on the task. Reading 100 highly cited optical studies in depth, we distinguish the design tasks in which artificial intelligence is irreplaceable, clearly advantageous, or without clear advantage. In our view, the key to the next decade is not more successes in isolated tasks but making each success a foundation for the field, through shifts such as shared data, trained models, and physics written into learning. Whether artificial intelligence leaves lasting value in this field will depend on whether its benefits can be verified, its methods transferred, and its designs corrected by experiment.

paper.title: Decay of space plasma turbulence downstream of bow shocks: MMS magnetosheath unbiased campaign observations
paper.summary: Turbulence properties in the solar wind change with increasing heliospheric distance. Observations from different missions have shown how spectral indices converge towards a $f^{-5/3}$ spectrum in the inertial range as the solar wind reaches one astronomical unit, and how the cascade rate decays as the plasma moves away from the Sun. We evaluate whether these properties display similar trends in a smaller astrophysical system, that of a planetary magnetosheath. Using data from the 2023 Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) unbiased magnetosheath campaign, we determine the evolution of the spectral indices and the cascade rate along 15 inbound magnetosheath crossings. WIND observations permitted to monitor the state of the solar wind during the campaign and allowed to study the impact of the upstream plasma conditions on the evolution of the cascade rate downstream the bow shock. Our results show an increase of the cascade rate between two to three orders of magnitude after the plasma crosses the bow shock into the magnetosheath. Once in the magnetosheath, turbulence develops with increasing distance to the bow shock in a way similar to solar wind observations, despite the smaller size of the system. Incompressible Hall-MHD scaling-law estimates of the cascade rate show a clear power-law decay of the cascade rate in the magnetosheath, particularly for the cases with upstream slow wind. This suggests that the way energy is injected into the system plays a role in the decay of turbulence as the plasma moves away from the bow shock.

paper.title: Chirality inversion and odd transport in a suspension of living rotors
paper.summary: Chiral symmetry breaking is a defining feature of life, visible at all scales from molecules to organisms. Yet how microscopic chirality propagates to shape the macroscopic properties of living matter remains poorly understood. Here, using a new experimental system of spinning microalgae, we show that a living chiral fluid behaves fundamentally differently from an externally driven one. As their density increases, cells self-assemble hydrodynamically into small rotating clusters which merge into a percolating chiral fluid. Strikingly, microscopic and macroscopic vorticity have opposite signs: individual cells all spin clockwise, yet clusters orbit counterclockwise. Combining experiments, theory and simulations, we show that both chirality inversion and percolation are direct consequences of the cells' internally driven nature. We then show how percolation reshapes transport, with even and odd diffusivities responding differently to the emerging network topology.

paper.title: Microscopic Theory of Spin-Orbit Interactions of Light
paper.summary: Optical spin-orbit interactions (SOI), demonstrated experimentally in optical cavities, enable the polarization degrees of freedom of light to be described and controlled as an effective pseudospin, providing a foundation for spintronic-like control of light and the development of next-generation optical technologies. However, prior works describe this emergent effect using phenomenological models that fail to uncover its microscopic quantum origins, and as a result, a rigorous connection between material electronic structure and the optical SOI remains elusive. In this work, we address this fundamental challenge by developing a microscopic quantum theory starting from the non-relativistic quantum electrodynamical (QED) description of light-matter interactions. We show that this effect arises from virtual interactions between confined photons and material excitations. Crucially, our theoretical framework provides microscopic material-design principles for tuning the distinct components of optical SOI, which include the optical birefringence, photonic self-energies, TE-TM splitting, and optical Zeeman splitting, enabling precise engineering of effective magnetic fields, diabolical points, and pseudospin textures. We anticipate that the predictive capability of our microscopic theory will enable systematic screening and design of material systems for photonic spintronics and optical technologies.

paper.title: Spectroscopic observations of periodic bursty ejections during a dome-spire-shaped jet
paper.summary:
Context: The study investigates the complexity of the formation and evolution of a dome-spire-shaped jet (or anemone jet) that originated in an active region and was presumably driven by null-point magnetic reconnection.
  Aims: We aim to provide a quantitative estimation of multi-temperature plasma dynamics and physical parameters of the jet and its blob-like features, together with its temporal evolution in three-dimensional perspective.
  Methods: For this, we analyze unique sit-and-stare spectral (Si IV, Mg II k, and C II) and slit-jaw imaging 1400 Å and 2796 Å observations obtained with the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), with a slit uniquely positioned just above the assumed reconnection site. Co-observations taken with the Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph of the Goode Solar Telescope in the chromospheric H$α$ and Ca II 8542.10 Å lines were also analyzed. These data are complemented by EUV imaging information from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory.
  Results: The IRIS observations reveal that the jet is formed by multiple periodic ($\sim$30 s) plasma ejections with blob-like appearance, each associated with strongly blueshifted Si IV 1402.77 Å transition-region emission reaching about $-300$ km/s. More importantly, the ejections are grouped into well-defined packets, each lasting approximately 3--5 min. In contrast, only a single Doppler component is observed in the chromospheric Ca II line. Multi-Gaussian decomposition of the Si IV line profiles reveals a highly accelerated plasma, with line-of-sight speed toward the observer increasing linearly from $\sim$30 to 112 km/s over 66 s, corresponding to an acceleration of 1.3 km/s$^2$. The kinetic energy release rate is estimated in the range of $\sim$1.0$\times10^{24}$--1.0$\times10^{25}$ erg\,s$^{-1}$.

paper.title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass
paper.summary: We develop a nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic (VEP) model for the stress-strain response of metallic glasses by connecting the deformation dynamics with the material relaxation time obtained from independent stress-relaxation measurements. The material is modeled as a Maxwell-type element, with a nonlinear elastic spring and a stretched-exponential dashpot whose behavior is determined from the separate stress-relaxation data. The model captures the effects of temperature and strain rate on the initial elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow. We independently determine the reference material-time function $X_0(\varepsilon)$ from the stress-relaxation response and the nonlinear material-time variable $X(\varepsilon)$ from the elastic-viscoplastic strain decomposition based on the stress-strain response. We introduce an Eyring-type function or material-time ratio $φ(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon)/X_0(\varepsilon)$ which quantifies the change of relaxation dynamics during nonlinear deformation. Our model provides a simple connection between structural relaxation and yielding in metallic glasses.

paper.title: Comparison of melanin subtypes using pump-probe microscopy
paper.summary: Pump-probe microscopy (PPM) is used to probe excited state dynamics of endogenous chromophores to generate contrast that is unavailable in traditional forms of microscopy. Here we apply PPM to characterize melanin, a pigment central to photoprotection, skin and eye pigmentation, and melanoma pathogenesis. Melanin is notoriously difficult to analyze due to its structural and chemical complexity. We imaged melanin from six different lesion categories: cutaneous nevi, lentigo, cutaneous malignant melanoma, conjunctival melanocytic lesions, vulvar melanocytic lesions, and a murine melanoma model, across 21 independent biological samples and 109 regions of interest. Using model fitting, adapted phasor analysis, and support vector machine classification, we characterize and quantify excited-state dynamics as a surrogate for chemical and structural heterogeneity. Heterogeneity of melanin separates cutaneous from non-cutaneous lesions, but is not correlated with malignancy. Benign lentigo is the most heterogeneous population in the dataset, exceeding cutaneous malignant melanoma, while conjunctival lesions are the most homogeneous despite receiving direct solar exposure. Classification on full transient absorption curves separates most subtypes well above the six-class chance level. These findings demonstrate the ability of PPM to reveal subtle differences in melanin photophysics across diverse tissue environments, with implications for optical tissue classification and the understanding of melanoma pathogenesis.

paper.title: Subsonic terahertz plasmon instability in space-time plasmonic crystals
paper.summary: We investigate collective plasma-wave dynamics in a two-dimensional electron fluid subected to a travelling periodic modulation of the effective plasma velocity. Using a hydrodynamic description combined with Floquet-Bloch theory, we show that the travelling modulation acts as a moving plasmonic crystal whose band structure is governed by an effective drift velocity in the comoving frame. We demonstrate that the closure of the Bragg gap at the edge of the Brillouin zone gives rise to an exceptional point and triggers a Krein-type instability through the coupling of positive- and negative-energy modes. Analytical expressions are derived for the instability threshold and growth rate, revealing that self-amplification can occur even when the electron drift remains subsonic in the laboratory frame. Numerical simulations of the nonlinear hydrodynamic equations confirm the theoretical predictions and show the evolution towards a saturated regime dominated by a coherent Floquet-Bloch mode. These results identify travelling plasmonic crystals as a novel platform for wave amplification and non-Hermitian band dynamics in electronic fluids.

paper.title: Frozen in Time: How a Physics Foundation Model Forgets Under Sim-to-Real Adaptation
paper.summary: Scientific foundation models (SciFMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of PDEs, including the ability to efficiently adapt to unseen data distributions with additional finetuning. As with all neural architectures, finetuning such models comes with the risk of catastrophic forgetting, whereby adapting to new tasks degrades prior knowledge of the model. We study catastrophic forgetting in Walrus-1.3B, a SciFM for continuum dynamics, over the course of a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation: first finetuning on simulated flow around a cylinder and then adapting to experimental data of the same system. We find that finetuning on the simulations rapidly degrades rollout performance on the original pretraining datasets, with one-step errors increasing up to 35x after just 20 epochs. Subsequent adaptation to real data further erodes performance on the simulated task. We characterize the potential drivers of forgetting, such as dataset dependence and task representation similarity. We then show that replaying as little as 1% simulated data during real-data finetuning recovers most of the lost simulation performance while retaining effective adaptation to the experimental dynamics. Our results identify catastrophic forgetting as a practical obstacle to sim-to-real adaptation of SciFMs and show that lightweight replay strategies significantly improve retention.

paper.title: Metadevices that compute: mathematical foundations and experimental implementations for neuromorphic nanophotonics
paper.summary: Wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a compelling alternative to digital electronics for specific linear-algebraic and machine-learning workloads, promising massively parallel, high-bandwidth, and energy-efficient information processing. Metamaterials, metasurfaces, and integrated metastructures (collectively, metadevices) now perform mathematical operations, solve integral and differential equations, multiply matrices, and implement trainable photonic neural networks directly in the wave domain. This focused review consolidates the mathematical foundations that underpin such devices, i.e., the mapping between linear operators and wave scattering, the feedback architectures that realize equation inversion, and the inverse-design and scientific machine-learning toolchains that make their synthesis and training tractable, and connects them to the rapidly growing body of experimental demonstrations, from free-space diffractive processors to reconfigurable guided-wave metastructures. We conclude with open problems and opportunities for this emerging neuromorphic nanophotonics ecosystem.

paper.title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
paper.summary: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.

paper.title: Dipolar Exciton Polarons in a van der Waals Homobilayer
paper.summary: Fermi polarons exemplify how many-body interactions give rise to emergent quasiparticles, providing a fundamental framework for understanding interacting quantum matter. In electron-doped two-dimensional semiconductors, exciton polarons offer optical access to Fermi-polaron physics and electrical tunability, yet achieving stronger and more controllable exciton-electron interactions remains a key challenge. Here, we realize dipolar exciton polarons in an electrically tunable van der Waals homobilayer, where interlayer excitons with spatially separated electrons and holes act as quantum impurities carrying permanent electric dipole moments. These dipolar polarons exhibit substantially enhanced exciton-electron interactions, with binding energies more than four times those of conventional intralayer exciton polarons. We further demonstrate that Fermi-sea layer polarization provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling many-body interactions. In particular, the presence of a Fermi sea induces hybridization between oppositely oriented dipolar polarons, whereas confining the Fermi sea to a single layer suppresses this hybridization and produces orientation-selective many-body dressing. Our findings establish an experimental platform for dipolar-polaron physics in which dipole orientation and Fermi-sea layer polarization jointly govern many-body interactions, opening a route towards electrically tunable interactions and dipolar-polaron-mediated attraction between itinerant electrons.

paper.title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
paper.summary: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.

paper.title: Cryogenic Optical Characteristics of S-FPL51 and S-LAH71: Refractive index, Transmission and Thermal expansion
paper.summary:
Several near-infrared instruments on upcoming extremely large telescopes use a combination of OHARA S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass prisms to correct for the atmospheric differential refraction. Because large parts of these instruments are contained within a vessel cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures, the changes in optical and mechanical properties should be considered during the design phase.
  In this report, we provide an update to our continuing efforts to characterize the S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass under cryogenic conditions. These efforts include a measurement of the refractive index (293 K, 100 K and 80 K), transmission measurements (293 K, 77 K and 43 K) and a determination of the coefficient of thermal expansion (between 293 K and 45 K). We will describe the cryogenic test setups that we have used to obtain our results, and provide summarizing equations of these material properties.
  This characterization will prove useful for conceptual design trade-offs, mechanical interface solutions and detailed optical design for future near-infrared instrumentation on large telescopes.

paper.title: Parametric Enhancement of an Optical Spring in a Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity
paper.summary: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.

paper.title: Quantum Advantage in Beam-Displacement Estimation for Inter-Satellite Quantum-Secure Time Transfer
paper.summary: In this work, we investigate the practical feasibility of achieving a quantum advantage, in the context of inter-satellite quantum communication, of satellite position estimation. The investigation focuses on a quantum-enhanced scheme in which squeezing is added to the derivative mode of a Gaussian probe beam as a means of estimating photon-beam displacement. The performance of the scheme is compared against the standard quantum limit achieved by an optimal classical beam-displacement estimation scheme under a fair same-total-energy constraint. We find that although the benefit provided by squeezing rapidly diminishes as the inter-satellite distance increases due to diffraction-induced beam spreading and subsequent truncation by the finite receiver aperture, a quantum advantage can still be expected over inter-satellite distances up to approximately 100 km under practical satellite configurations. This distance scale between satellites is anticipated for Starlink-type satellite constellations.

paper.title: Spectral Information Content of Diffraction-Limited Images
paper.summary: High-resolution optical imaging is fundamentally limited by diffraction, which imprints wavelength-dependent structure onto the point spread function (PSF) of the optical system. This intrinsic chromaticity implies that in addition to spatial structure, images encode spectral information. We develop the theory of this spectral information content and provide strategies for its optimal extraction with calculations of Fisher information. We show that polychromatic PSF formation can be expressed as a convolution in logarithmic coordinates and define the corresponding spectral transfer function. We derive this function for the Airy disk and find algebraic decay in spectral log-frequency, implying the existence of arbitrarily fine spectral structure in the ideal, noiseless PSF. We use a differentiable forward model to numerically construct the spectral information eigenbasis and quantify the spectroscopic capability of diffraction-limited imaging across a range of noise and detector systematics. We demonstrate injection and recovery of the constrained spectral modes in a realistic simulated example and compare these results with previously reported methods. Our information-theoretic framework provides a generalisable method for spectral characterisation of PSFs spanning a variety of imaging contexts.

paper.title: The spin-transfer inverse Faraday effect in Au/YIG thin film bilayers
paper.summary: The inverse Faraday effect (IFE) (the generation of an effective magnetic field in a material upon irradiation with circularly polarized light) offers a pathway to ultrafast, non-thermal control of spin dynamics. In metallic/ferromagnetic-insulator (NM/FMI) bilayers, IFE-driven spin polarization in the metallic layer can be an alternative to generate magnon excitations in the magnetic insulator which otherwise would be inaccessible with photon energies below the insulator bandgap, but this avenue has remained mostly unexplored. In this work, we investigate the regime of spin-transfer via IFE in Au/YIG bilayers, by means of ultrafast time-resolved magneto-optical experiments. Understanding the mechanism of this spin-transfer IFE in these NM/FMI heterostructures is crucial for several reasons: it elucidates the fundamental coupling between light's angular momentum and collective spin modes at buried interfaces, it enables all-optical generation and manipulation of pure spin currents, and it paves the way toward THz-frequency spintronic devices leveraging the insulator's long magnon lifetimes.

paper.title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
paper.summary: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.

paper.title: Beam Transport Through a Quadrupole with Offsets in Both Transverse Planes
paper.summary: In accelerator switchyards with shared magnets, a beam may traverse a quadrupole with offsets in both transverse planes, a configuration that cannot be represented by a single conventional horizontal or vertical combined-function bend. Such an off-axis quadrupole bends the reference trajectory and generates dispersion simultaneously in both planes. We derive a compact analytical $6\times6$ transfer matrix about the curved reference trajectory. The model is formulated in Bishop coordinates using a weak-curvature approximation that retains the longitudinal variation of both reference-curvature components and the resulting dispersion in both transverse planes. The analytical linear model is compared with a sliced representation based on conventional second-order combined-function bend maps and with direct numerical integration of the Lorentz equations in the ideal Cartesian quadrupole field.

paper.title: Report of the National Lab Accelerator Study Group for a Muon Collider
paper.summary: The National Laboratory Accelerator Study Group (NLASG) was established to assess the accelerator research and development required to advance a future high-energy Muon Collider, with particular emphasis on opportunities for coordinated contributions from U.S. national laboratories. This report examines the principal accelerator subsystems, their technical maturity, and the critical challenges that must be addressed before proceeding to a technical design. Topics include the proton driver, target and capture system, muon cooling, acceleration, collider ring, and machine-detector interface. The study identifies priority R&D activities, evaluates opportunities to leverage existing laboratory capabilities and accelerator infrastructure, and outlines a staged approach to technology demonstrations and integrated system validation. Particular emphasis is placed on developing a coordinated national research strategy that complements international efforts and establishes a technically credible path toward a future Muon Collider.

paper.title: High-transformer-ratio plasma-based afterburner for extending X-ray free-electron laser photon energies to $\gtrsim$50 keV
paper.summary: Bright coherent X-rays in the $\gtrsim$50 keV range are highly desirable for applications in materials science, high-energy-density physics, and nuclear physics, but are difficult to obtain from present X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) facilities. Plasma-based afterburners offer a compact route to increasing the electron-beam energy, yet high transformer ratio (TR) operation is vulnerable to hosing instability, which can severely degrade the witness beam quality. We propose using a transversely elliptical driver beam to excite an elliptical nonlinear plasma wake with an axially varying focusing gradient, thereby suppressing the witness beam hosing through betatron decoherence. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations show that, for a 3 kA driver and a 2.35 kA witness beam with an rms length of 4 $\mathrmμ$m and a beam separation of 94 $\mathrmμ$m (TR $\approx 3$), this scheme can accelerate an 8 GeV witness beam to $\sim30$ GeV while nearly half of the electrons meet the XFEL requirements. Start-to-end simulations show that the resulting beam can drive $\gtrsim50$ keV XFEL radiation with peak powers of $\sim10$ GW and durations of $\sim10$ fs, even when quantum diffusion is included, offering a compact route to extend existing XFEL facilities to higher photon energies.

paper.title: Estimation of Very High Energy Electron (VHEE) beam parameters using an in-air screen
paper.summary: Very high energy electron (VHEE) beams offer several promising properties for radiotherapy. Accurate beam delivery requires a beam model that accounts for scattering along the beam propagation path. This work develops and validates a beam model incorporating Multiple Coulomb Scattering (MCS) to estimate beam parameters. MCS is incorporated as an additive term to the covariance matrix transformation for a drift space, allowing conventional quadrupole scans to estimate beam parameters in the presence of a downstream scatterer. The scattering correction factor is fitted to Monte Carlo (MC) simulations for a range of materials and thicknesses. The model is then validated by recovering the initial beam parameters from simulated quadrupole scans of a realistic beamline. Finally, the method is applied to in-air screen measurements at the Pulsed Energetic Electrons for Research (PEER) end station of the Australian Synchrotron. After fitting the correction factors, the mean and standard deviation of the estimation errors for the final emittance, diameter, divergence, and mean kinetic energy were $(-0.06 \pm 3.17)\%$, $(0.15 \pm 0.66)\%$, $(0.18 \pm 2.18)\%$, and $(-0.03 \pm 0.06)\%$, respectively. Simulated quadrupole scans successfully recovered the initial beam parameters, with errors of at most $13\%$. PEER measurements yielded emittance estimates ranging from $0.238$ to $1.753~\mathrm{mm\,mrad}$ across scans, which were within the expected range. Following an initial quadrupole scan, the method allows the in-air beam size to be estimated for other quadrupole configurations. Further work is required to improve the consistency and reliability of the experimental estimates.

paper.title: High-Efficiency Wakefield Acceleration of Positrons via a Slit Plasma Channel
paper.summary: Although plasma-based wakefield acceleration has achieved remarkable success for electrons, efficient positron acceleration remains a long standing challenge, as positrons suffer severe defocusing in the accelerating phases of such structures. Here, we propose a slit plasma wakefield acceleration (SPWA) scheme, in which a relativistic electron beam propagating through a slit channel formed by two parallel plasma slabs excites crossing plasma-electron filamentary structures within the slit, generating intense wakefields tailored to simultaneously provide longitudinal acceleration and transverse focusing for a trailing positron bunch. A theoretical model is developed to characterize the wakefield structure responsible for positron acceleration and focusing. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations validate the model, and demonstrate that the SPWA scheme achieves a positron trapping efficiency of nearly 100%, while maintaining low emittance growth and narrow energy spread for an injected positron beam. These findings establish a new and robust approach to high-efficiency positron acceleration, with promising implications for future compact electron-positron colliders and high-energy positron applications.

paper.title: Hydrogen Electron Cyclotron Resonance Dissociator Demonstrator for the Project 8 Experiment
paper.summary: Project 8, a neutrino mass experiment, employs the novel frequency technique of cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy (CRES) to perform a model independent measurement of neutrino mass via tritium beta decay. Our pioneering experiment will consist of a beamline that dissociates molecular tritium, surface cools atoms through accommodation, evaporatively cools and slows atoms, and traps them in a CRES resonant cavity to advance towards our sensitivity goal of 40 meV/c^2 for our final electron-weighted neutrino mass measurement. We are prototyping an electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) dissociator that uses a tunable 1 kW 2.45 GHz RF generator and electromagnets to ignite a hydrogen plasma in an aluminum resonant cavity. Our ECR source is designed to produce a high atom flux (~10^19 atoms/second) near room temperature. We present the engineering development, gas diagnostics, and spectroscopy data from our hydrogen plasma.

paper.title: Single-pass stochastic cooling for electron microscopy
paper.summary: Scientific applications of free electrons, such as in electron microscopes and particle accelerators, are limited by the brightness of available electron sources. Accelerators can use phase space cooling to surpass these source limitations, whereas electron microscopes can only rely on particle filtering to increase beam coherence at the cost of reduced brightness. We show that strong electron-light coupling in nanophotonic structures makes it possible to achieve single-pass stochastic cooling inside an electron microscope for a lossless improvement of longitudinal emittance. This approach is laser-free and compatible with normal CW operation of electron microscopes. We derive a fully quantum mechanical model of stochastic cooling valid in the strong coupling regime, finding an analytic asymptotic formula for the optimal cooled energy spread $σ_{E_f}\simeq0.88(\hbarω)^{2/3}σ_{E_0}^{1/3}$, with $\hbar ω$ the cooling photon energy and $σ_{E_0}$ the initial energy spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the energy spread reduction is reflected in an increase in the purity of the electron's quantum state and a reduction of the longitudinal phase space area. Our work paves a path towards even brighter beams for electron microscopy, promising higher image quality, enhanced spectral resolution, and a route to reaching fundamental quantum limits on electron beam phase space area.

paper.title: Impact of Rapid Acceleration on Beam Dynamics in the Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons of a Muon Collider
paper.summary: Circular muon colliders offer a promising route to multi-TeV centre-of-mass energies with high luminosity. The baseline design for the high-energy complex includes a chain of four Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons (RCSs) accelerating the beam from \qty{63}{\GeV} to \qty{5}{\TeV}. The chain combines a conventional synchrotron with three hybrid synchrotrons, which use fixed-field superconducting dipoles and rapidly ramped normal-conducting dipoles. The short muon lifetime (\qty{2.2}{\micro\second} in the rest frame) imposes stringent constraints on the acceleration process: achieving the target luminosity requires a muon survival rate of up to \qty{70}{\percent} throughout the acceleration chain, with the full acceleration completed in approximately \qty{10}{\milli\second}. These demanding acceleration conditions raise several beam-dynamics challenges, investigated in this work. First, the impact of the RF cavity distribution on transverse emittance growth is studied. Second, the mismatch between the discretely increasing beam energy and the continuously ramped fields of the pulsed dipoles and quadrupoles is modelled analytically, and its impact is evaluated through tracking simulations. Finally, the sensitivity of the beam trajectory, optical functions, and emittance growth to magnetic-field ramp jitter is assessed.

paper.title: Cryogenic suppression of correlated loss in Rydberg atom arrays
paper.summary: Blackbody radiation (BBR) poses a central challenge for quantum science with Rydberg atoms. By driving transitions to nearby opposite-parity states, BBR shortens Rydberg lifetimes and has long been suspected to trigger "avalanche" events known to cause correlated atom loss. Here, we suppress avalanche decay and establish BBR as its dominant trigger using a Rydberg atom array that operates either cryogenically or at room temperature. A $45~\text{K}$ radiation shield reduces ambient BBR, extending Rydberg $nS$ lifetimes for $n$ ranging from 50 to 75. BBR-induced decay rates are suppressed by 30%-50%, corresponding to an effective blackbody temperature $T_{\rm eff}\approx190~\text{K}$. This enables controlled comparisons of Rydberg-dressed atom arrays operating in different BBR environments. Arrays of up to 70 atoms demonstrate cryogenically suppressed avalanche rates, tracking the suppression in BBR-induced decay, for both $n=50$ and $n=60$ dressing. A parameter-free rate model agrees with the measured avalanche rates after accounting for frequency-dependent cryogenic shielding, photoionization-triggered avalanches, laser phase noise, BBR decay channels, and Rydberg interaction effects. We demonstrate a quantitative description of avalanche decay and show that improved BBR shielding should further suppress correlated loss to the $T_\text{eff}=45~\text{K}$ achievable in the current apparatus. Our results establish a route to mitigating correlated errors that otherwise impede fault-tolerant operation in neutral-atom quantum processors.

paper.title: LADA: A differential algebra-based simulation package for arbitrary-order charged-particle and light optics
paper.summary: LADA computes charged-particle and light-optical transfer maps by differential algebra in Python, with run-time order selection validated through order nine. It combines these established map methods with ATIMA-based stopping, straggling and scattering, the GLOBAL, CHARGE and ETACHA charge-state models, EPAX fragmentation, six-dimensional integration through measured or computed RF fields with reference-energy rebasing, and section-wise particle tracking with aperture and RF-window losses. Maps retain analytic dependence on external parameters; contraction with input moments gives beam observables and their sensitivities without particle tracking at each setting. Lattice import from COSY, MAD-X, Xsuite and MIRKO provides per-record status and comparisons with available codes. NumPy is the only required dependency. On the HHT benchmark, the optional compiled DA kernel on eight cores matches COSY in performance at orders 3 and 5 and is 1.8 and 2.9 times faster at orders 7 and 9. Applications include the SIBAF irradiation facility through CALINA, proton microscopy and beam-line studies at GSI and FAIR.

paper.title: Nuclear recoil with electron vacuum polarization in muonic atoms
paper.summary: Using the heavy-particle QED approach, we derive the last missing $α\,(Zα)^5\,m^2/M$ nuclear recoil correction in muonic atoms, which originates from the combination of the $(Zα)^5\,m^2/M$ recoil with the electron vacuum polarization. Numerical results are presented for the $1S$, $2S$, and $2P$ states of $μ$H, $μ$D, $μ^3$He$^+$, and $μ^4$He$^+$. For the $2P-2S$ Lamb shift in muonic helium ions, our results are of opposite sign and about four times smaller in magnitude than the previous logarithmic estimates.

paper.title: OPALX: A performance-portable framework for particle accelerator simulations
paper.summary: Accurate charged-particle beam simulations require self-consistent collective fields and realistic accelerator models, while their computational cost motivates efficient use of heterogeneous computing systems. We present OPALX, a performance-portable accelerator simulation framework that builds on the beam-dynamics capabilities of OPAL. Its modular architecture uses the Independent Parallel Particle Layer (IPPL) and Kokkos to support distributed-memory execution on multicore CPUs and GPUs from a common codebase. The framework combines relativistic particle tracking with prescribed accelerator fields, particle-in-cell space charge calculations, and spin tracking. We describe the physical and numerical models and their integration into the simulation workflow. The implementation is assessed using disorder-induced heating and frozen-spin test cases, together with comparisons of spin evolution with G4Beamline and beam transport with TraceWin. A three-dimensional space charge benchmark evaluates throughput on CPU and GPU systems, reaching approximately $10^9$ macroparticles per second on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for this benchmark. These results provide initial verification of the implemented models and demonstrate CPU and GPU execution of self-consistent space charge calculations. OPALX provides a common foundation for extending accelerator models and numerical methods across heterogeneous computing platforms.

paper.title: The two-loop Lamb shift: the final missing contribution
paper.summary: The last significant unknown contribution to the two-loop Lamb shift, namely the electron self-energy with vacuum-polarization insertion into the photon line, is determined including higher-order effects in the parameter $αZ$, with $α$ being the fine-structure constant and $Z$ the nuclear charge number. Our calculation improves the accuracy of theoretical predictions for energy levels and transition energies in heavy hydrogen-like and lithium-like ions by up to one order of magnitude, enabling more stringent comparisons between theory and available experimental results. These results pave the way for more precise tests of quantum electrodynamics in the strong-field regime, as well as for accurate determinations of nuclear charge radii.

paper.title: Discovering like a scientist: Literature-informed dimensionless learning for physical closure of data-driven equations
paper.summary: Data-driven methods can recover compact equations, yet the physical dependence of their coefficients across operating conditions often remains unresolved. Dimensionless groups can explain this variation, but selecting relevant groups from the many dimensionally admissible combinations remains challenging. Here, we introduce a knowledge-guided framework for dimensionless learning, called π-former. It learns patterns of variable association and exponent assignment from a corpus of 1,288 established dimensionless groups. Under exact dimensional constraints, the model proposes interpretable basic groups whose combinations are optimized against observations. Across seven physical problems, the framework identifies predictive dimensionless coordinates within seconds. Integration with equation discovery further expresses condition-dependent coefficients through these coordinates, recovering established physical scalings in multi-condition simulations. Applied to experimental measurements of evaporation-driven wetting, the framework discovers dimensionless coordinates and uses them to construct a unified trajectory equation. The resulting model generalizes to held-out conditions across liquids and initial volumes, outperforming existing empirical models. These results establish dimensionless learning as a transferable bridge between accumulated scientific knowledge and data-driven equation discovery, enabling artificial intelligence to uncover physically meaningful laws from observations.

paper.title: Inverse modelling of a laser-plasma accelerator
paper.summary: The electron beams of a laser-plasma accelerator depend non-linearly on the laser and gas settings. This dependence is explored using particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations, and machine-learning models trained on these simulations predict the beam from the settings. Here we address the reverse problem: given a measured beam, which settings produced it? We infer three of them: the gas pressure $p\_1$, the normalised vector potential $a\_0$ and the nitrogen concentration $c\_{N\_2}$. The solution is not guaranteed to be unique. We train an ensemble of mixture density networks that, for each beam, output several possible sets of settings with their probabilities and uncertainties, and test them on simulated beams with realistic measurement noise. On average, the predictions are accurate ($R^2 = 0.91$), yet for about two-thirds of the beams the inferred distribution has two competing solutions. These share nearly the same value of $a\_0^2 p\_1$, which controls how strongly the laser focuses itself in the plasma and, in earlier PALLAS studies, when electrons start to be injected. Keeping this quantity fixed gives beams that are practically indistinguishable with realistic diagnostics. A forward model used as a check removes unphysical solutions but cannot choose between the two plausible ones. We then test two ways to resolve the ambiguity. Adding the full electron energy spectrum improves the mean prediction ($R^2 = 0.94$), mostly through $a\_0$. It changes the weights of the two solutions but does not move them. A second measurement at a deliberately different plasma density is more effective. In paired PIC simulations, it reduces the error on $a\_0$ by a factor of 2.6, whereas repeating the measurement at the same density brings almost no gain.

paper.title: Sympathetic Cooling of Ionic Fullerenes with Ultracold Atoms to Millikelvin Temperatures
paper.summary: Cooling complex molecular ions to millikelvin temperatures remains a major challenge because their intricate internal structures prevent laser cooling. Here, we propose to use an ultracold gas of Cd atoms to efficiently cool C$_{60}^+$ ions to average kinetic energies of approximately 20 mK, following an initial precooling stage with He buffer gas. Our approach is based on full molecular dynamics simulations using accurate ion-atom interaction potentials derived from high-level electronic structure methods. Furthermore, using a Monte Carlo approach, we predict the formation of C$_{60}^+$ Coulomb crystals supported solely by collisions with the buffer gas. The probability of reaching these cold states shows a pronounced dependence on the number of trapped ions, revealing the competition between neutral-atom cooling and many-ion dynamics in radio-frequency traps.

paper.title: Quantum Spin Wave Theory with Multi-Spin Interactions for Magnetic Materials Modeling
paper.summary: In the field of magnetism within condensed matter physics, magnetic systems are microscopically described by a spin Hamiltonian. Its parameterization is accessible through both ab initio calculations and fits to experimental data. Frequently, this is achieved via multi-stage calculations that either relate the parameters to observable material properties or map a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto an effective spin model. In this realm, accurate and flexible methods are essential for simulating the physical properties of the latter. The present study focuses on one such method: spin wave theory. The approach is applied to a new formulation of the spin Hamiltonian, named polynomial localized spin model (PLSM), which includes terms of arbitrary order in the spin operators. This enables the direct application of linear spin wave theory (LSWT) to the analysis of the energy landscape and spin-wave spectrum of arbitrary collinear and non-collinear phases in any realistic magnetic material. Moreover, the classical and quantum parts of the PLSM are cleanly separated. Finally, an open-source implementation of LSWT, named Magnopy, is presented. It interfaces with modern parameterization software, supports arbitrary collinear and non-collinear systems, and is designed for both scripting and standalone use.

paper.title: Numerical Study of Two-Frequency Heating in ECR Ion Source
paper.summary: The two-frequency heating (TFH) method is widely used to improve the performance of electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) ion sources, yet its physical mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. In this work, the TFH regime in the DECRIS-PM ECR ion source is studied numerically using the NAM-ECRIS code. Single-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz (500 W) is compared to two-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz and 13 GHz (450 W + 50 W) at equal total power. It is found that while the global plasma parameters remain largely unchanged, the peak density of highly anisotropic electrons (E > 1 keV, Vperp/Vlong > 10) decreases by ~20% and their distribution broadens radially in the TFH regime. This reduction in electron anisotropy is attributed to the randomizing effect of the lower-frequency wave on electron gyromotion, which suppresses plasma micro-instabilities and leads to improved ion production.

paper.title: Photoionization rates of oxygen and nitrogen at 800 nm measured by Thomson coherent microwave scattering
paper.summary: In this study, we report on the use of Thomson coherent microwave scattering (CMS) to characterize photoionization rates in oxygen and nitrogen at 800 nm over a range spanning approximately three orders of magnitude, from about mid-10$^9$ s$^{-1}$ range to the to mid-10$^{12}$ s$^{-1}$ range, corresponding to laser intensities in the vicinity of 10$^{13}$-10$^{14}$ W/cm$^2$, a range of significant practical relevance to filamentation physics.

paper.title: Energy-Guided Transport for Projection-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching
paper.summary: Deep generative models, particularly Flow Matching frameworks, have emerged as powerful tools for synthesizing complex physical systems. However, standard architectures remain purely statistically driven and agnostic to the underlying governing equations, often violating fundamental physical constraints during inference. Existing zero-shot approaches designed to enforce these constraints typically rely on rigid algebraic projections. While effective for sparse boundary conditions, applying such discrete geometric corrections to dense, full-domain PDEs may disrupt the probability path, \rev{potentially deviating from the learned manifold and introducing substantial computational overhead}. To address these challenges, we introduce Energy-Guided Transport, a novel training-free framework that formulates non-linear physical constraints as a smooth potential energy landscape. Rather than interrupting the ODE integration, our method applies a continuous dissipative force directly to the intermediate generative states, steering them toward the physical manifold. By evaluating this force implicitly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation, our framework preserves the natural dynamics of the flow while maintaining an efficient $\mathcal{O}(N)$ algorithmic complexity.
