Particle image velocimetry (PIV) requires uniform tracer seeding and undistorted particle images, and cavitating flow violates both, because tracers do not penetrate vapor structures and refractive index mismatch across deforming interfaces produces spurious vectors. We present a domain-adapted deep optical flow framework for two-phase velocimetry, built on a Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms (RAFT) architecture fine-tuned on synthetic image pairs rendered from multiphase OpenFOAM simulations (RAFT-CloudCav). It is evaluated against a pre-trained generalist RAFT model, Farnebäck and OpenPIV on 130,000 frames/s recordings of a Venturi test section at 30 and 48 L/min. As no experimental ground truth exists, validation uses three quantities that require none, namely the integrated flow rate against a turbine meter, the liquid-phase velocity divergence, which mass conservation requires to vanish, and the station-to-station spread of the flow rate. RAFT-CloudCav recovers 47.75 L/min against a metered 48.0 $\pm$ 0.5 L/min, the closest of the four methods, and its flow rate varies by 2.0% across four streamwise stations, versus 6-7% for the classical methods. It returns a coherent near-wall reverse flow of -0.71 m/s, the time-averaged signature of the upstream-propagating re-entrant jet, where OpenPIV returns none. In the non-cavitating control, at 51 $μ$m/pixel only three grid points fall inside a 0.68 mm boundary layer and the peak wall-normal gradient is under-predicted more than thirtyfold, while 13 and 19 $μ$m/pixel agree with each other. The mean field is recovered without tracer particles at roughly three times the per-frame uncertainty. Uncertainties are estimated a posteriori from the image residual and propagated conservatively.

paper.title: Layer-Peeling Inversion of Temporal Refractive Index Profiles from Noisy Data
paper.summary: We introduce a direct method for reconstructing the temporal evolution of a medium from electromagnetic field measurements. A sequence of temporal refractive-index changes splits an incident wave into forward- and backward-propagating components, producing a \emph{spatial} response of finite extent. We show that this finite support, together with causality, enables sequential reconstruction of the temporal interfaces through a time-domain extension of layer peeling. For continuously varying media, we introduce a time-adjusted Goupillaud medium and, through space-time duality, establish the corresponding momentum-conservation and admissibility conditions. The method remains robust under incomplete and noisy measurements, providing a general framework for the metrology, characterization, and design of time-varying electromagnetic systems.

paper.title: Existence of Distinct Strong and Weak Shear Regimes of Self-Generated Turbulent Magnetic Reconnection
paper.summary: Magnetic reconnection can become fast in three-dimensional turbulent layers. However, the parameters and mechanisms that control the fast state are not yet fully clear. Existing guide-field simulations of self-generated turbulent reconnection show locally coherent flux-rope structures embedded in a stochastic layer, motivating a flux-rope-mediated picture, with reconnection rates of order $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.01$ in MHD. Here, we test whether and how magnetic shear changes the reconnection regime, using 3D resistive-MHD simulations at $S_L=10^5$. We vary the guide field while keeping the initial reconnecting field strength and rate normalization fixed, comparing a guide-field, weaker-shear configuration with the anti-parallel, strong-shear limit. We find that the strong-shear regime is qualitatively distinct from the flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime. Rather than retaining a narrow layer and locally coherent flux-rope structures, the current layer develops short-wavelength corrugations that broaden it substantially, and the reconnection layer electric field is sustained by fluctuation EMF. The reconnection rate increases to $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.03$, about three times the guide-field value. These results indicate that magnetic shear can select the mechanism controlling fast 3D turbulent reconnection, shifting the system from a guide-field regime consistent with flux-rope mediation toward a very fast turbulence-broadened regime. This transition provides a novel explanation for the sudden switch-on of fast reconnection in eruptive solar flares.

paper.title: Sub-filter-scale stress and heat flux in hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer
paper.summary: A comparative study of sub-filter-scale (SFS) quantities in hypersonic Couette flow and flat-plate boundary layer turbulence under strongly cooled-wall conditions is carried out using filtered direct numerical simulation (DNS) data to characterize the differences in SFS dynamics between internal and external wall-bounded turbulence. The two flows exhibit similar near-wall behaviour in the mean velocity profiles and SFS stress components; however, marked differences emerge in the outer layer and thermal structure. The two configurations also exhibit different thermal fields, leading to different temperature-velocity relations. The SFS behaviour shows strong sensitivity to the filtering operation: the top-hat filter yields larger SFS magnitudes, whereas the sharp spectral filter preserves a distinct spectral separation near the cutoff, leading to characteristic SFS features. Decomposition of the SFS terms shows that the residual component provides the dominant contribution to the mean SFS shear stress and heat flux. Differences between the two flows are primarily associated with the interaction terms between the resolved and residual components, which contribute with opposite signs in the two configurations, consistent with their different thermal structures. The different thermal structures also lead to distinct SFS heat-flux behaviour, including a sign change in the flat-plate boundary layer. Instantaneous SFS fields further reveal that local extrema arise from the combined contributions of multiple decomposed terms. Although these terms exhibit large local fluctuations, their net contributions to the averaged SFS quantities are relatively small. The trace of the SFS stress exhibits local negative values, reflecting local energy redistribution across the filter scale rather than a loss of physical energy.

paper.title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
paper.summary: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.

paper.title: An Analytical Model for Laser-Activated Two-Phase Choking and Microfluidic Suction on Surface Boundary Layers
paper.summary: We present a predictive fluid mechanics model to calculate pressure drops (0.25 atm) and fluid velocities (2.50 m/s) governed by localized phase change and choking phenomena in a capillary-constrained, coaxial microfluidic actuator. Driven by near-infrared thermal absorption, the analytical framework describes how energy deposition drives vapor cavity growth and subsequent cavitation bubble collapse, inducing a transient suction force across a curved, two-radii Young-Laplace capillary boundary. Velocity drops are derived from closed-form analytical equations that explicitly couple vapor volume dynamics with non-linear flow area restriction and fluid drag. The model predicts a maximum boundary layer wall shear stress of 30.06 Pa at the target interface. Crucially, this shear magnitude matches the physical threshold required to mechanically strip surface contaminant boundary layers while remaining below the damage threshold of underlying target substrates. Finally, we formulate a closed-form expression for the maximum allowable liquid inlet temperature required to prevent thermal saturation and sustain stable, continuous microfluidic suction cycles. These equations establish direct engineering design rules for optimizing phase-change microfluidic actuators and next-generation coaxial fluidic systems.

paper.title: TwinLight: A Multi-Timescale Physical-Layer-Aware T-API-Compliant Optical Domain Controller Digital Twin
paper.summary: We demonstrate TwinLight, an open-source optical-network digital twin acting as an optical domain controller. Its T-API REST and telemetry streaming interfaces expose a physical-layer engine that combines a GNPy steady-state baseline with four analytical transients.

paper.title: Breathers across the Focusing-to-Defocusing Transition: From Diffraction-Like Dynamics to Talbot Carpets
paper.summary: We experimentally investigate fundamental unstable breather wave groups propagating across the transition from focusing to defocusing regimes. In hydrodynamics, this transition is realized through a rapid reduction in water depth over a short spatial interval. We demonstrate that the time-periodic Akhmediev breather develops a Talbot-like recurrence pattern in the defocusing regime, although only its initial stages are experimentally accessible. In contrast, the Peregrine breather exhibits qualitatively different behavior, characterized by oscillatory envelope dynamics. These oscillations can be understood as a purely linear phenomenon arising within the nonlinear Schrödinger framework when dispersion dominates over nonlinearity, as further confirmed by numerical simulations over extended propagation distances. The experimental observations agree closely with finite-depth nonlinear Schrödinger predictions across regimes with substantially different relative strengths of dispersion and nonlinearity. Our findings reveal a temporal analogue of diffraction and provide a foundation for exploring focusing-to-defocusing transitions in other nonlinear dispersive media.

paper.title: Redetermination of the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BaMgF4
paper.summary: BaMgF4 (BMF) has the potential to serve as a platform material for vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) nonlinear optics owing to its ferroelectricity and high UV transparency down to 130 nm. However, the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients reported for BMF span approximately one order of magnitude, hindering a reliable assessment of its potential for nonlinear optical applications. Here, we redetermined these coefficients by combining Maker fringe, wedge, and single-pass second-harmonic-generation measurements at a fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm. Our results establish that all the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BMF lie in the range of 0.01-0.04 pm/V. We determined d31 to be 0.035 pm/V, which is among the largest coefficients of BMF, while it has been underestimated relative to the other coefficients in previous studies. Although d31 is not the largest coefficient, the use of its long corresponding coherence length is beneficial for quasi-phase matching, particularly for VUV generation, where the fabrication of lower-order quasi-phase-matching structures is crucial.

paper.title: Evaporation-induced colloidal diffusiophoresis in electrolyte solutions
paper.summary: Non-volatile solutes accumulate near a receding drying front, generating concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport by diffusiophoresis. This dynamic spatial arrangement of colloidal particles could affect the microstructure and macroscopic properties of the dried film. Here, we combine experiments and theory to investigate polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. By varying the electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, we show that evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid-gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. We use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface and couple it to particle transport to capture the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends. These results identify background electrolytes and drying rate as coupled controls on particle distribution and provide a predictive framework to optimize formulation and processing parameters for manufacturing slurry-based materials, such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.

paper.title: When is an Optical Design Problem a Mass Transfer Problem?
paper.summary: This paper investigates whether optical design problems can be represented as Monge--Kantorovich mass transfer problems with some cost function. An optical problem is specified by a function defining a particular family of supporting surfaces for the optical element. We introduce the notion of geometric equivalence between optical and transport problems, which is directly related to the possibility of formulating an optical design problem as a mass transfer problem. A necessary condition for such equivalence is derived in the semi-discrete setting. It allows a transport representation to be ruled out without choosing a cost function in advance. The condition is applied to the near-field refractor problem and to the design of two refracting surfaces transforming a spherical beam into a spherical or collimated beam. For these problems, the necessary condition is shown to fail in physically admissible configurations. We also study an optical element with a single working surface and an arbitrary regular incident wavefront. In the far field, geometric equivalence to a mass transfer problem requires a planar or spherical wavefront, whereas in the near field with a planar target, the necessary condition fails for an arbitrary smooth wavefront.

paper.title: An acousto-optic colorimeter for color psychophysics
paper.summary: A complete model of human color perception requires the ability to present any color as a stimulus.Most existing measurements were collected with physical color samples, and current laboratory generators, such as displays and multi-primary LED systems, work with a small number of fixed primaries. Published color-difference data therefore cover about 40\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram, while commercial wide-gamut displays already reach two thirds of it and need difference metrics there. We describe an acousto-optic colorimeter that lets the experimenter choose the primaries. The device selects up to four narrow bands from a supercontinuum (white-light) laser, each with electronically set wavelength and intensity, and covers 95\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram. Threshold-scale color differences, presented in alternation as in a discrimination experiment, are reproduced with a mean error of 0.08--0.12 CIEDE2000 units ($ΔE_{00}$) at five CIE-recommended color centers. Because one color can be built from many combinations of narrow bands, the bands are chosen for the task: the finest adjustment for color matching, the least disagreement between observers for color-difference measurement. In simulations with 151~individual observers from a published dataset, with these bands observers see colors 0.6--1.9~$ΔE_{00}$ from the intended one on average, against 1.2--2.5~$ΔE_{00}$ on a calibrated wide-gamut LCD, lower at every center. The approach applies to any narrowband source and lets experimenters use saturated colors while limiting the effect of individual differences in color vision.

paper.title: Raytracing and quantifying the inferior mirage
paper.summary: Using custom raytracing code, we explore several features of the inferior mirage that are not widely discussed, such as the blurring in the mirage image, and what happens to the light in the direct image region that is replaced by the mirage image. The raytracing model also clarifies how to quantify the mirage, and we provide expressions to calculate the angular extent of the mirage under given thermal conditions and measurement geometry.

paper.title: Optical microscopy for pathological imaging: past, present, and future
paper.summary: Histopathology, the microscopic examination of stained tissue sections, remains the gold standard for pathology imaging, but its bright-field imaging is largely morphological. Advanced optical microscopy techniques move beyond this by exploiting diverse light-matter interactions, and are increasingly applied to pathological imaging. By capturing signals such as refractive index, polarisation, harmonic generation, Brillouin shift, and molecular vibrations, these microscopy techniques can provide quantitative or semi-quantitative information on tissue structure, mechanics, and chemical or molecular composition. In this review, we summarise the physical principles, key quantitative parameters, and representative pathological applications of seven modalities--optical diffraction tomography, polarisation microscopy, second-harmonic generation microscopy, third-harmonic generation microscopy, Brillouin microscopy, Raman microscopy, and fluorescence microscopy. We also discuss progress in artificial intelligence that supports reconstruction, analysis, and interpretation across these modalities, together with emerging trends in multimodal integration. Overall, this review shows how different optical contrasts can complement routine histopathology, while outlining the challenges and opportunities that will shape their clinical translation.

paper.title: Self-injection-locked dark-soliton Kerr optical frequency combs with high even-order normal dispersion
paper.summary: We numerically investigate dissipative dark-soliton (DDS) microcombs under the action of pure high even-order normal (HEON) dispersion in a microresonator with the self-injection locking (SIL). Pure 4th, 6th, 10th, and 14th-order normal dispersion can support DDSs formed by interlocked switching waves, directly excited through a SIL-based turnkey scheme without detuning sweeps. Compared to the pure 4th-order case, the switching-wave tail oscillation period increases and its decay rate decreases with the increase of the dispersion order. Although the overall comb bandwidth narrows, the number of non-pump comb lines above a common absolute power threshold increases. Furthermore, the feedback phase controls the DDS duty cycle and intracavity comb-line power distribution, while the increase of the pump power improves the estimated pump-to-comb output conversion efficiency.

paper.title: Differential chiral sensing at exceptional points in intrinsically chiral metastructures
paper.summary: Discriminating opposite enantiomers through their weak chiroptical responses remains a fundamental challenge in optical sensing. Exceptional points (EPs), non-Hermitian singularities at which eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, offer a route to enhanced spectral responses through their characteristic square-root eigenvalue splitting. However, their potential for chiral discrimination remains largely unexplored. We demonstrate exceptional points in an intrinsically chiral hybrid metamaterial and reveal strongly asymmetric responses to enantiomeric perturbations. The interplay between intrinsic chirality and non-Hermitian degeneracy is realized through the coupling of a chiral plasmonic nanoantenna array to a photonic crystal slab. We observe characteristic complex-square-root scaling, with both resonance frequencies and loss-rates exhibiting pronounced handedness dependence. Remarkably, opposite enantiomers produce complex mode splittings that differ by more than an order of magnitude. Our findings establish intrinsic chirality as a new degree of freedom in non-Hermitian physics and reveal a fundamental route toward topological singularities enhanced discrimination of chiral matter.

paper.title: Laser-Direct-Written polymer WGM microring laser integrated on a fiber tip for refractive index sensing
paper.summary: Whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microlasers are promising for refractometric sensing, but their practical implementation can be limited by the need for stable resonator-coupler alignment. Here, we demonstrate a Rhodamine B-doped polymer WGM microring laser directly fabricated on an optical-fiber tip, eliminating the external resonator-fiber coupling interface at the sensing head. Micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing are combined for fabrication, while finite-difference time-domain simulations guide the microring laser design. The microlasers operate in air and water with thresholds of 0.224 uJ and 0.458 uJ, respectively. Refractometric measurements in aqueous glucose solutions yield a bulk refractive index sensitivity of 364.95 nm/RIU and a detection limit of 2.47 x 10^(-4) RIU. Water-induced polymer changes and photobleaching are also investigated. This fiber-tip architecture provides a basis for probe-based refractometric sensing in environmental and biochemical applications.

paper.title: Deep-UV All-dielectric qBIC Metasurface for Refractive Index Sensing
paper.summary: All-dielectric metasurfaces supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) have emerged as powerful platforms for biosensing, yet their operation remains largely concentrated in the visible and near-infrared regimes. Extending these resonances into the deep-ultraviolet (DUV) to probe the intrinsic electronic absorption of biomolecules presents substantial material and nanofabrication challenges. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a hafnium dioxide (HfO$_{2}$) metasurface supporting DUV qBICs in the wavelength range from 225 nm to 340 nm with quality factors reaching 500. We further demonstrate its refractive index sensing capabilities through integration with a microfluidic cell and optical characterization in reflection mode. We show that the introduction of an aqueous buffer leads to a further quality factor enhancement. Achieving a sensitivity of up to approximately 60 nm/RIU and an operational figure of merit of 40 $\mathrm{RIU}^{-1}$, this low-loss HfO$_{2}$ metasurface provides a robust foundation for label-free DUV biosensing.

paper.title: Modulation Induced Memory Resonances in Dynamically Driven Optical Cavities
paper.summary: Temporal modulation of optical cavities provides a powerful mechanism for controlling photonic states beyond the static cavity paradigm. Here, we investigate the dynamics of periodically driven optical cavities using a time-dependent cavity-field model with modulated resonance frequencies. We demonstrate modulation-induced tuning of cavity resonances and analyze the resulting intracavity field evolution in both amplitude and phase. The interplay between periodic modulation and cavity dissipation gives rise to pronounced hysteretic behavior, revealing memory effects associated with the finite photon lifetime of the cavity. By quantifying the hysteresis area as a function of modulation frequency, we identify distinct memory resonances characterized by enhanced field-history dependence at specific driving frequencies. Furthermore, we examine the time-resolved local density of optical states (LDOS) and show that temporal modulation enables dynamic spectral redistribution of photonic states, with the degree of confinement governed by the cavity loss rate. Our results establish a simple framework for understanding and engineering memory effects in dynamically driven optical resonators and provide new opportunities for tunable photonic environments, dynamic LDOS control, and reconfigurable light-matter interactions.

paper.title: Tailoring resonator geometry for astigmatism compensation with structured light in birefringent optical cavities
paper.summary: In this work, we experimentally investigate the astigmatism induced by a birefringent crystal inside an optical cavity and demonstrate a geometric compensation strategy for structured modes carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). We show that the astigmatism observed in the semimonolithic configuration can be fully compensated by introducing a third mirror to fold the cavity, thereby exploiting the geometric astigmatism arising from oblique incidence on the curved mirror. By performing a study of the resonator geometry, both theoretical and experimental results confirm that this approach enables the preservation of OAM between the pump beam and the converted signal and idler modes, providing an effective design strategy for birefringent optical cavities.

paper.title: Discrete time crystals and heteroclinic switching in actively mode-locked semiconductor lasers
paper.summary: We investigate the mechanisms underlying the emergence of discrete time crystals in actively mode-locked semiconductor lasers. Our analysis is based on a Haus master equation generalized to retain carrier memory between round-trips. We perform a detailed bifurcation analysis that reveals a well-defined hierarchy of subharmonic states, illustrating how pulses may suppress their neighbors when the modulation runs faster than the pulse round-trip frequency. To identify the underlying mechanism, we derive effective equations of motion that couple the pulse energies, their positions relative to the modulation transmission maxima, and the local time-dependent gain. These reveal that transitions between time-crystalline states occur via transcritical global bifurcations, opening a regime of heteroclinic winnerless competition between symmetry-degenerate configurations.

paper.title: Universal photonic synthetic temporal-mode converter for heterogeneous quantum interconnects
paper.summary: We propose a synthetic temporal-mode converter (STC) that combines programmable waveform matching with denser time multiplexing for heterogeneous quantum interconnects. Programmable couplers and optical delays reshape known single-photon temporal waveforms through coherent interference between time bins. Conversion to a common single-bin mode concentrates amplitudes from $N$ bins in $\lceil\log_2N\rceil$ mixing stages, simultaneously improving temporal indistinguishability and freeing channel time. Simulations yield mode overlaps above 99.9\% for exponential and Gaussian inputs. For $N=256$ and $0.5\,\mathrm{dB}$ loss per stage, STC gives a 45.6-fold higher photon-pair coincidence rate than temporal gating at equal mode overlap for two exponential inputs. Relative to long pulses, the shortened temporal matched mode can support an approximately 41-fold higher photon-pair coincidence rate when the available time-multiplexing capacity is fully utilized.

paper.title: Shaping Frequency-Bin Biphoton Correlations via Programmable Optical Frequency Combs
paper.summary: Programmable shaping of photon-pair spectral correlations is important for frequency-bin quantum information processing. However, achieving this control remains challenging in nonlinear optical systems without reliable forward models. Here, we demonstrate model-free, hardware-in-the-loop shaping of the measured joint spectral intensity of a cascaded photon-pair source driven by a programmable optical frequency comb. A blockwise simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation controller optimizes up to 22 pump, signal, and idler parameters. Each iteration requires only two accepted hardware evaluations, independent of the parameter count. The controller converges to diverse target patterns on 3$\times$3, 4$\times$4, and 5$\times$5 frequency-bin grids. The optimized distributions achieve Pearson correlations between 0.66 and 0.98 and classical overlap fidelities between 0.32 and 0.62. Cross-target similarity analysis confirms that the optimized patterns remain target-specific. Source characterization yields a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio of approximately 585. Accuracy is limited by pump-phase transfer, parasitic nonlinear background, waveshaper constraints, amplitude-only filtering, and measurement noise. Joint spectral intensity contains no spectral-phase information. Therefore, the results demonstrate control of measured frequency-bin populations and correlations, not complete reconstruction of the two-photon state. Phase-sensitive characterization is required to verify inter-bin coherence and quantify the entanglement dimensionality of the output state. Our results establish direct measurement feedback as a practical approach to reconfigurable frequency-bin correlation engineering when an accurate end-to-end model is unavailable.

paper.title: Cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation from Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O
paper.summary: Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O provide a solid-state setting for creating giant optical nonlinearities. Here, we use second-harmonic generation (SHG) to study Rydberg excitons in a doubly resonant optical microcavity designed to enhance both the pump and second-harmonic fields. We observe even-parity exciton states in an optical cavity and extend cavity-based measurements of Rydberg excitons up to $n=10$. The SHG intensity depends strongly on pump cavity detuning, showing the dominant role of the microcavity is the enhancement of the intra-cavity pump field. Analysis reveals an additional enhancement from the resonant second-harmonic cavity giving an overall SHG enhancement factor of $21 \pm 2$ inside the microcavity. These results establish cavity-enhanced SHG spectroscopy as a valuable tool for studying Rydberg excitons in microcavities and provide a pathway towards exploiting optical nonlinearities in Rydberg exciton polariton systems.

paper.title: Inversion symmetry breaking by interlayer hybridization in a tetralayer van der Waals heterostructure
paper.summary: Inversion symmetry breaking unlocks a broad range of physical phenomena fundamental for modern technologies, motivating efforts to engineer noncentrosymmetric materials. In this context, monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, which naturally lack inversion symmetry, have emerged as a versatile platform for valley physics, strong excitonic effects, and nonlinear optics. However, in their hexagonal stacking phase, inversion symmetry is restored in even-layer stacks and bulk form, suppressing these effects and limiting applications. In this work, inversion symmetry breaking is demonstrated in a vertically stacked tetralayer heterostructure assembled from two intrinsically centrosymmetric bilayer flakes, as evidenced by second harmonic generation measurements with an intensity comparable to that of their constituent monolayer. Spectroscopic measurements and theoretical estimations indicate that effective symmetry breaking in the tetralayer heterostructure is driven by interlayer hybridization, giving rise to pronounced electronic and phononic signatures. This symmetry breaking further induces polar anisotropy, with an intensity ratio reaching 2.36. We propose that asymmetric contributions from excitons to the second harmonic optical dipole may influence this behavior. These findings establish interlayer coupling as a critical mechanism for introducing inversion symmetry breaking and tuning the optical response of van der Waals heterostructures, providing a powerful strategy for photonics and optoelectronics in two-dimensional materials.

paper.title: Absolute Calibration of a Broadband Transmission Grating Spectrometer from 5 to 400 nm with Uncertainty Estimates
paper.summary: We present the absolute calibration of a transmission grating spectrometer (TGS) with uncertainty estimates in the 5--400 nm range using synchrotron radiation at the BEAR beamline at Elettra light source in Trieste, Italy. Firstly, the spectral responsivity of a Si photodiode in the spectrometer was absolutely calibrated with respect to the absolutely-calibrated beamline photodiode. Subsequently, this photodiode was used to calibrate the transmittance of Zr and Al thin-film filters, along with bulk MgF$_2$ and UV-grade fused silica windows at their operating positions in the spectrometer to minimize mounting-induced uncertainties. Next, the quantum efficiency of the spectrometer's CCD camera was calibrated over the 5--400 nm range. Lastly, three gratings with line densities of 10000, 3000, and 1000 lines/mm were calibrated for spectroscopy in the ranges extending from soft X-ray to extreme-, vacuum- and deep-ultraviolet (DUV) wavelengths, respectively. The combination of various filters and gratings enables absolutely calibrated spectroscopy with high versatility across a broad wavelength range from soft X-rays to DUV.

paper.title: Disentangling Spin and Orbital Contributions in the Search for Altermagnetic Terahertz Conversion in RuO2
paper.summary: Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a prominent candidate altermagnet, yet the microscopic origin of its reported charge-angular-momentum conversion remains unsettled. Recent theoretical and experimental advances have highlighted a potentially dominant role of orbital transport, raising a fundamental ambiguity between spin- and orbital-mediated conversion in RuO2. Here, we report the first experimental disentanglement of the spin- and orbital-to-charge conversion channels in RuO2 heterostructures using terahertz emission spectroscopy. We identify Fe as a predominantly spin-current injector, whereas Ni and permalloy predominantly inject orbital currents, revealing a substantial orbital contribution to ultrafast terahertz emission. Under controlled spin-current injection, we find no evidence for inverse altermagnetic spin-splitting effect. Instead, the observed anisotropy is consistent with an anisotropic inverse spin Hall response that is strongly conditioned by the near-interface environment. Under orbital-current injection, the anisotropy is markedly weaker, indicating that orbital-to-charge conversion is largely isotropic in RuO2. Our results establish orbital transport and interface-conditioned spin Hall conversion as key to terahertz emission from RuO2, underscoring the need to disentangle spin, orbital, and interfacial contributions before assigning anisotropy to altermagnetism.

paper.title: Talanov dynamics and chirp-controlled rogue-wave formation for the vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation
paper.summary: We study the focusing vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation, or Manakov system, for a pair of coupled initial conditions with compactly supported, concave parabolic density profiles and phases depending quadratically on the spatial coordinate. We focus on the natural class of self-similar solutions generated by such profiles, whose dispersionless evolution we refer to as Talanov dynamics. We extend the criterion for blow-up in finite time, first established for a single field, to the Manakov case. For arbitrary initial chirps in the two fields, we provide closed-form expressions for their evolution, and an explicit expression for the time of the gradient catastrophe, if it occurs, and we classify the effect of the coupling on the catastrophe. Depending on the initial chirps, the two fields may catastrophise, or relax, as each would if decoupled. However, coupling can also force the catastrophe in fields that would otherwise relax if decoupled. For identical initial supports, and in the presence of dispersion, we numerically show that the same dispersionless criterion determines, in the semiclassical regime, whether the fully dispersive solution relaxes or develops a rogue wave in each field, whose onset time is accurately predicted by the corresponding dispersionless catastrophe time, in direct analogy with the scalar case. As chirp and amplitude are relatively easy to control experimentally, we expect these results to be relevant to experiments in nonlinear optics and Bose-Einstein condensates, extending to coupled systems observations made for the scalar equation.

paper.title: Physics design of a dual-ring light source toward MHz-rate free-electron laser radiation
paper.summary: Combining the high peak brilliance and short pulse duration of free-electron lasers (FELs) with the high repetition rate of diffraction-limited storage rings (DLSRs) is a promising direction for accelerator light sources. In this paper, we propose a dual-ring light source concept that, at MHz repetition rates, delivers pulses with a pulse durations and peak power intermediate between those of FELs and DLSRs. Such a light source can be realized as an upgrade of an existing DLSR by adding an isochronous ring equipped with transverse gradient undulators (TGUs) and connecting the two rings via bunch compression and decompression systems. We present the conceptual layout and show that bunch compression shortens the electron bunches to ps-scale durations; multi-turn radiation in the isochronous ring raises the repetition rate to 1.36 MHz from a single TGU; and the long TGUs enhance the brilliance, delivering $10^{7}$--$10^{9}$ photons per pulse across the soft and hard X-ray range, an increase of 2--4 orders of magnitude over the original DLSR. The dual-ring light source thus provides a cost-effective route to MHz FEL operation based on existing storage-ring infrastructure, combining the high repetition rate of a DLSR with the short pulses and high brilliance of a linac-driven FEL.

paper.title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 2: intensity effects and beam instabilities
paper.summary: In this lecture, dealing with intensity effects, the equations of longitudinal motion with induced beam voltage are analyzed. This allows us, first, to describe the single-bunch potential well distortion and the loss of Landau damping. Then the linearized Vlasov equation is used to derive step-by-step the Lebedev equation. This matrix equation is then applied to find the thresholds, growth rates and spectra of an unstable multi-bunch beam. The lecture is concluded by a discussion of possible beam-instability cures.

paper.title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 1: single and double rf systems
paper.summary: In the first part of this lecture, the main characteristics of synchrotron motion, namely, synchronous particle and phase, bucket area and emittance, are introduced. The equations of longitudinal particle motion in a single rf system of a proton synchrotron are rederived and the phase equation is analyzed for small and large amplitude particles. The particle motion below and above transition energy is also considered. The main applications and operation modes of a double rf system are discussed in the second part of the lecture. The intensity effects and beam instabilities are the subject of the following lecture.

paper.title: Symplectic Normal Coordinates Flow for Generative Modeling of Hamiltonian Systems
paper.summary: In conditioned generative models of physical systems, the densities at different values of the conditioning parameters are often related through symplectic transformations. For stable linear Hamiltonian systems, there exists a symplectic transformation to "normal coordinates" such that the dynamics is reduced to rotations in each phase-space plane. This picture extends to the nonlinear case where, away from resonances, the Birkhoff normal form again consists of rotations in phase space, now with amplitude dependence. In this work, we introduce an invertible symplectic flow layer consisting of amplitude-dependent rotations in learned normal coordinates. We derive the condition under which the nonlinear rotation layer is symplectic and detail an architecture that guarantees it. Experiments are carried out on three conditional generative modeling problems: a synthetic chain of coupled nonlinear oscillators and two problems from accelerator physics. We show empirically that normalizing flows with the new layers achieve competitive or superior negative log-likelihoods compared to baseline flows, with gains that grow with the strength of the nonlinearity on the synthetic system.

paper.title: Status of Accelerator Automation in the Community: Classification, Survey Results, and the Role of AI and Machine Learning
paper.summary: The increasing complexity of particle accelerators and the growing demand for operational efficiency have intensified the focus on automation in accelerator control systems. However, there is still a lack of a common language to describe and compare the level of automation across different facilities. This article presents a generic classification scheme for accelerator automation, defining five distinct levels ranging from basic operational assistance to full autonomy. To assess the current state of automation in the accelerator community, a structured survey was conducted during the 14th Workshop on Accelerator Operations (WAO 2025). Responses from major laboratories indicate that more than one third of accelerators currently operate at the lowest level 1 (operational assistance), and no facility has yet reached full automation. However, projections show a clear trend toward higher levels within the next decade. Key drivers include optimization algorithms for autotuning, finite-state machines, and closed-loop feedback systems. This study provides both a conceptual framework and a snapshot of current implementation practices, supporting a shared understanding of accelerator automation across the community.

paper.title: Optimizing an RFSoC LLRF Controller for a Low-PRF, Short Pulse System
paper.summary: The Advanced Light Source (ALS) LINAC operates with 3 GHz RF pulses at 0.7 Hz pulse repetition frequency (PRF) and 1.2 microsecond duration, imposing severe limitations on traditional PID and adaptive feedforward control schemes. An RFSoC-based controller prototype was developed and presented in prior work to upgrade the legacy LLRF systems for the LINAC and Subharmonic Buncher. This paper presents sampling scheme optimizations and interleaving calibration techniques for RFSoC based control of pulsed RF systems. We detail bench characterization methodologies to isolate component-level phase noise across individual ADC, DAC, and clock components in the Xilinx ZCU208 hardware ecosystem. Finally, we explore translating open-loop controller bench measurements into controller-added closed-loop LLRF performance predictions.

paper.title: Physics in Safety and Safety in Physics: Lessons from the LHC and its Underground Experiments
paper.summary: Large underground particle-physics facilities are usually discussed by separating scientific performance from the systems that make their operation safe. We develop a complementary view in which safety is treated as an intrinsic part of the physical and operational structure of an experiment. Using the LHC, ATLAS, and CMS as principal case studies, we introduce the concepts of physics in safety and safety in physics: physical laws, measurements, and models determine hazards and protective barriers, while those barriers in turn define the machine, detector, access, and intervention states in which physics can be performed. We formulate this relation through a \emph{safe operational phase space} and through admissible trajectories connecting different configurations, emphasizing that safety constrains not only states but also transitions between them. The framework is applied to beam and magnet protection, cryogenic and oxygen-deficiency hazards, detector-specific risk configurations, personnel access, maintenance, and radiation protection, with particular attention to the different architectures of ATLAS and CMS. We argue that validated protection does not merely restrict scientific activity but can enlarge the domain of sustainable operation. This viewpoint provides a unified physical and operational framework for understanding safety at the LHC and for incorporating protection, maintainability, and recoverability into the design of future accelerator and underground facilities such as HL-LHC, FCC and muon collider.

paper.title: Beam-beam effects on measurements at electron-positron colliders: LEP neutrino counting and Higgs factories
paper.summary: Beam-beam electromagnetic interactions affect the luminosity, collision energy, polarization, and particle backgrounds relevant to precision measurements at electron-positron colliders. We investigate these effects using Fast $e^{\pm}e^{\pm}$ Beam and Luminosity (FeeBL), a new beam-beam simulation framework, and compare its predictions with published results from LEP and proposed future colliders. We reproduce the analytical field-integration calculations of LEP Bhabha scattering and identify an approximately 2% bias in previously published beam-deflection simulations. Applying the corresponding luminosity correction and a revised uncertainty assessment motivated by the observed agreement among the four LEP experiments yields ($N_ν= 2.9965 \pm 0.0040$), compared with the previously reported ($2.9963 \pm 0.0074$). The revised uncertainty is conditional on an assumed common rescaling of experiment specific uncertainties and motivates further investigation of the original uncertainty budgets. We identify and correct implementation errors in the modeling of Breit-Wheeler, Bethe-Heitler, and Landau-Lifshitz pair production, with implications for detector backgrounds at Higgs factories. Simulated beam depolarization and luminosity spectra are compared with existing ILC and HALHF predictions. Finally, we investigate collision energy monochromatization for direct Higgs production, obtaining sub-MeV collision energy peak widths in exploratory linear collider configurations at substantial luminosity cost, while finding significantly weaker narrowing for the FCC-ee configurations studied. We derive a rigid Gaussian beam overlap model and estimate that FCC-ee needs roughly 10 m of horizontal only dispersion to reach widths of $\approx1~\mathrm{MeV}$.

paper.title: Effects of pulse durations in atom interferometry with double Raman diffraction
paper.summary: Double Raman diffraction is a key enabling technique for future space missions relying on atom interferometry that offers enhanced sensitivity and intrinsic suppression of systematic effects. This diffraction mechanism naturally arises when employing a retro-reflection configuration in microgravity, but then accelerations can no longer be determined through a frequency-chirp scan. As a consequence, measurements become much more sensitive to systematic effects associated with pulse timing and duration. Indeed, the finite pulse duration can introduce additional phase shifts and small modifications of the arm trajectories, which are critical sources of error in high-precision measurements. In this work, we present the first complete analytical results of these effects for double Raman diffraction, building upon previous work for single diffraction and extending the standard literature. Our analysis determines the impact of finite pulse durations on the full interferometer sequence, quantifying the shifts of the atomic wave packets' trajectories and the acquired phases. The description relies on a comprehensive framework describing matter-wave propagation in terms of central trajectories and centered wave packets, and can be easily incorporated into relativistic treatments. Furthermore, we make use of group theoretic methods that are particularly useful when accounting for residual accelerations and frequency chirps, which are also relevant for ground-based applications. Our study includes time-dependent accelerations and frequency chirps, gravity gradients, retardation effects, AC Stark shifts induced by the Raman pulses, and external forces such those due to magnetic fields or temperature gradients in the black-body radiation.

paper.title: HFR distorted-wave photoionization of Te III: a preliminary benchmark for large-scale atomic data production to model nebular-phase kilonovae
paper.summary: The shortage of photoionization cross sections for heavy elements remains an obstacle to non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) modeling of nebular-phase kilonova ejecta, where hydrogenic prescriptions have often been adopted in the absence of ion-specific calculations. We present a first preliminary benchmark of direct photoionization cross sections for doubly ionized tellurium, obtained using the distorted-wave (DW) approximation within the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock (HFR) method implemented in the Cowan codes, in which a semi-empirical adjustment based on the observed energy levels is performed. For the photoionization from the ground level of Te III to the ground level of Te IV, comparison with Dirac R-matrix data shows encouraging agreement in the magnitude and overall decrease of the non-resonant background in the lower photon-energy region, approximately below 4 Ry (autoionizing resonances are absent from the present direct treatment). These preliminary results support HFR distorted-wave calculations as a promising and computationally tractable approach for large-scale production of photoionization cross sections, with lanthanides and actinides as longer-term targets, in light of their importance to kilonova modeling and of the severe lack of atomic data for these species.

paper.title: Rapid high-purity loading of barium ion via relayed selectivity from naturally abundant source
paper.summary: Trapped ions is one of the promising platforms for realizing quantum information processing and quantum simulation. Selective and rapid loading of a specific isotope lays the critical foundation for such purpose particularly when scaling up the system size. Here we demonstrate a new method for rapid isotope-selective loading of $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ or $^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$, two types of promising ion qubits, from naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme. Neutral atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm $6s^2\,{}^1S_0\rightarrow6s6p\,{}^3P_1^o$ transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to $6s6d\,{}^3D_1$, and ionized using an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts shows relayed selectivity that the second step can further suppress undesired-isotope excitation and no contaminant ion is detected during our entire experiment. Besides, the resonant drive of the second step excitation yields a prominent loading rate of the selected species. This strategy using multi-step excitations to establish relayed selectivity can be extended to high-purity loading of other species of ions.

paper.title: Consistent Mapping for Fluid Structure Interaction with Geometrically Nonlinear Isogeometric Beams
paper.summary: Isogeometric beam formulations provide an efficient reduced-dimensional representation of slender structures, combining accurate geometry and high-order continuity with few structural degrees of freedom. Their application to fluid--structure interaction (FSI) requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. While mapping strategies exist for conventional finite element beams, geometrically nonlinear isogeometric formulations require operators consistent with their spline-based kinematics and distinct descriptions of cross-sectional rotation. This work develops consistent beam-to-surface mappings for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned FSI. Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified through analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek--Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark. The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, while demonstrating the applicability of both beam formulations to coupled FSI problems.

paper.title: High-sensitivity sensing technology of 10 MHz radio frequency electric field based on Rydberg atoms
paper.summary: To address the pressing need for high-sensitivity, miniaturized electric field sensors in the short-wave communication band (3-30 MHz), this study proposes and demonstrates a radio frequency electric field quantum sensing scheme based on cesium atomic Rydberg states and the electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) effect. The scheme employs an all-infrared optical design, utilizing 852 nm probe light, 1470 nm dressing light, and 780 nm coupling light to efficiently prepare the 49P3/2 Rydberg state in a room-temperature cesium vapor cell, which is then probed non-destructively via ladder-type four-level EIT spectroscopy.

paper.title: Efficient sensitivity analysis for combustion problems via reformulation and adjoint methods
paper.summary: Numerical simulations of combustion processes rely on chemical kinetic models, whose predictive capability is typically assessed by comparing measurements of quantities of interest (QoIs) in idealized experimental configurations with the corresponding simulated values. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the influence of model parameters on QoIs, making it a key tool for model development and optimization. Given the large number of parameters involved in detailed kinetic models compared to the number of QoIs, adjoint methods are a promising approach for efficient sensitivity analysis. Ignition delay times (IDTs) and extinction strain rates (ESRs) are among the QoIs of primary importance. However, applying adjoint methods to these quantities is not straightforward and is addressed in this work. The system of governing equations is reformulated via a coordinate transformation that makes the QoI an explicit component of the solution vector. This reformulation enables the application of adjoint sensitivity analysis for both IDT and ESR. A computational complexity analysis demonstrates that the proposed formulation significantly improves algorithmic efficiency compared to conventional approaches. The methodology is verified by comparing adjoint sensitivity coefficients with those obtained from other methods. Execution time measurements show computational cost reductions of up to two orders of magnitude relative to standard direct sensitivity analysis. A benchmark study is conducted across kinetic models of increasing size to assess how far theoretical efficiency gains are realized in practice. While the results show that implementation details can limit performance for smaller problem sizes, the expected asymptotic scaling is observed for larger models. The benchmark thus provides a reference framework for identifying key performance bottlenecks and guiding subsequent optimization efforts.

paper.title: Offline Evaluation of Information-Theoretic Adaptive Bayesian Vector Magnetometry
paper.summary: An information-theoretic adaptive Bayesian framework for jointly estimating the longitudinal and transverse components of a magnetic field from the time-resolved optical response of a cold $^{87}$Rb ensemble is presented. A linearly polarized continuous-wave probe drives the $D_2$ $F{=}1 \rightarrow F'{=}0$ transition, producing coherent population trapping (CPT) lineshapes whose width, contrast, and transient dynamics depend sensitively on the ambient magnetic field. The full temporal signal, including early-time transient signal and the steady-state absorption, is compared against a precomputed Maxwell-Bloch forward model. The joint posterior distributions of the longitudinal and transverse components of the magnetic field are updated sequentially, while marginalizing over instrumental nuisance parameters arising from the finite resolution of the magnetic bias coil supply. At each step, the applied longitudinal bias field is chosen to maximize the expected Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the current prior and the anticipated posterior, the expected information gain. As a proof of principle, the protocol is validated in post-processing on pre-recorded experimental scans, and both field components converge to well localized field estimates with weak correlation between them, consistent with the distinct dependence of the CPT resonance position and lineshape on the field components. These results establish an information-theoretic framework for joint vector field estimation from transient cold-atom spectroscopy. However, there exists a systematic forward-model discrepancy, showing that posterior concentration alone does not establish accuracy and motivating nuisance-parameter inference in future online implementations.

paper.title: GPU acceleration of the numerical-atomic-orbital DFT code OpenMX with GEMMul8: performance and numerical agreement on consumer and HPC GPUs
paper.summary: We integrate GEMMul8, a library that emulates FP64 matrix multiplication on INT8 Tensor Cores, into the GPU version of the numerical-atomic-orbital first-principles code OpenMX 4.0. The GEMMul8 configuration is compared against the cuBLAS FP64 configuration within each of two environments, a consumer GeForce RTX 5080 and an HPC-oriented H100 PCIe, for the four computational paths formed by collinear (CL) or noncollinear (NCL) spin and band or $Γ$-point-cluster solvers. In fixed-work measurements that completed 25 SCF iterations, the diagonalization section of a 384-atom CL band calculation on the RTX 5080 is accelerated by a factor of 2.1 and the total run time by 1.8; a 512-atom CL cluster calculation, which uses only real matrix products in contrast to the CL band calculation, still gains a factor of 1.5 in the diagonalization section. On the H100, GEMMul8 provides little additional acceleration of the diagonalization section. In an accuracy test on a 216-atom Si system in which one atom was displaced by 0.05 angstrom, all 24 configurations were converged using an SCF convergence criterion of $10^{-8}$; every configuration converged at the same iteration within each path, and the differences between GEMMul8 and cuBLAS are at most $2\times10^{-12}$ Ha in the total energy and $7\times10^{-12}$ Ha/Bohr in force components.

paper.title: A versatile beamline for attosecond photoelectron and photon spectroscopy
paper.summary: We report on the development of a versatile attosecond beamline for ultrafast spectroscopy of atoms and molecules, as well as for the metrology of infrared laser pulses. Using a few-cycle pulse (approximately 5 fs) for driving the high-order harmonic generation process, we show that the modulation of the harmonic flux in the cut-off spectral region, induced by a weak perturbing field, enables complete electric-field characterization of the perturbing pulse. Phase-sensitive detection with a lock-in amplifier further reveals polarization-dependent effects, observed as modulations at twice the fundamental optical frequency, emphasizing the sub-laser-cycle electronic control inherent to the measurement technique. In addition, the beamline supports the implementation of two-color (extreme ultraviolet and infrared) phase-sensitive experiments using approximately 30 fs pulses and a velocity map imaging spectrometer (VMI). This configuration will enable the study of photoemission time delays in atomic and molecular systems. Together, these results establish the beamline as a robust and adaptable platform for probing attosecond dynamics across diverse experimental approaches.

paper.title: Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions for the Spectral Difference method on simplex elements
paper.summary: Unsteady compressible simulations with high-order methods on unstructured meshes require boundaries that let acoustic, entropy and vorticity waves leave the domain without spurious reflection. For the spectral difference (SD) method, the Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions (NSCBC) have only been formulated on quadrilaterals and hexahedra. Their strong-form formalism relies on a line of flux points normal to the boundary face, which does not exist on triangles and tetrahedra. This paper extends the NSCBC to the SD method on simplex elements, including multi-species reacting gases. The characteristic analysis is performed in the physical frame of each flux point of the boundary face, and the normal derivative of the normal flux is evaluated using the Raviart-Thomas divergence operator. The boundary fluxes are recovered from a linear system local to each boundary element, whose matrix depends on the geometry only. The treatment is compared with the tensor-product formulation at a comparable number of degrees of freedom on a series of test cases covering acoustic, vortical, viscous and reacting flows on triangles and tetrahedra. In all cases, the results are in close agreement with those obtained on quadrilaterals and hexahedra, so that the NSCBC become available for the SD method on simplex meshes, which are well suited to complex geometries.

paper.title: Dynamics of singular-jet formation during the collapse of drop-impact craters
paper.summary: The collapse of a drop-impact crater that bypasses the pinch-off singularity produces exceptionally thin, high-velocity jets, often referred to as singular-jets. We perform 2D axisymmetric DNS using Basilisk, employing adaptive mesh refinement to capture the intricate flow features. The numerical results for a drop diameter of $3.64$ mm at ambient pressure match the experiments well under different impact conditions. During the crater collapse, qualitatively different dimple shapes form, including an entrapped bubble beneath the dimple. Quantitatively, an entrapped bubble with a diameter of ~210 μm and a jet velocity of 61.7 m/s for the singular-jet case during cylindrical dimple collapse is obtained from simulations. Subtle morphological changes in crater evolution distinguish the jetting regime, with a critical angle of 109.2 between the crater side wall and its base in the singular-jet case. The simulation provides insight into the internal flow fields, enabling us to delineate the observed phenomenon. The pressure and velocity fields reveal that the high jetting velocity is associated with the formation and rapid collapse of a nearly cylindrical dimple. The resulting pressure distribution drives a strongly upward flow near the dimple base, while the nearly parallel dimple side walls redirect radial liquid motion towards the axis. We extend the simulations into the post-entrainment region and identify another singular-jet near the upper boundary of the entrainment region. The jet reaches a velocity of 63.93 m/s and exhibits morphological characteristics similar to the first singular-jet case. A regime map is constructed from simulations spanning Weber numbers ranging from 100 to 200 and Froude numbers from 45 to 92; the updated lower and upper boundaries for the entrainment region, based on singular-jet formation, are We = 45.5\, Fr^{0.237} and We = 53.5\, Fr^{0.251}, respectively.

paper.title: On the Method of Projection onto Localized States for Describing Reactions and Clustering
paper.summary: The method of projection onto localized states intended for describing reactions and clustering is examined. In particular, the method offers a simple extension of the no-core shell model to continuum- and clusterized bound states. A critical analysis of a previous realization of the method is provided. A way to minimize the number of basis functions required for convergence is given. An easy way to obtain exactly unitary and symmetric $S$ matrix from calculations is pointed out. The method is tested in one- and two-channel $np$ scattering problems with the Daejeon $NN$ interaction. It is shown that excellent convergence can be reached even when only oscillator states with low number of excitation quanta are retained.

paper.title: Finite temperature and pressure structural relaxations including zero-point motion and anharmonicity
paper.summary: At finite temperature and pressure, the equilibrium structure of a crystal minimizes the Gibbs free energy rather than the static Born-Oppenheimer energy. We present WARP (Wyckoff-constrained Anharmonic Relaxations at Pressure and temperature), a symmetry-constrained, variable-cell relaxation based on the stochastic temperature-dependent effective potential method, including anharmonicity and zero-point motion. Every position update is projected onto Wyckoff positions and every strain onto symmetric strains, so a relaxation can raise the symmetry but never lower it. For aluminum, the thermal expansion follows measurements at cryogenic temperatures, including the quantum plateau below 50 K. For lanthanum hydrides at megabar pressures, equations of state agree with phonon-based and path-integral calculations, and LaH$_{10}$ relaxes from its rhombohedral static minimum to the observed cubic phase, also with a machine-learned potential fine-tuned on 150 supercells. For brucite, Mg(OD)$_2$, lattice parameters, bond distances and thermal expansion agree with neutron diffraction, and the O-D isotope effect is captured.

paper.title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows
paper.summary: Numerical simulation of hypersonic vehicles is an attractive approach to investigate the complex phenomena involved in such technologies. For this, second-order finite volume methods (FVM) are the established method in computational fluid dynamics, with the cost of high dissipation in affordable meshes, thus needing refined ones or adaptive mesh refinements techniques to obtain accurate results. An alternative is to make use of high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, in particular discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM), once it achieves higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases. Therefore the goal of this work is to present the numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration to test and verify the applicability of the DGSEM approach for a complex hypersonic flow where shock-shock interactions occur. Results revealed to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thus verifying the code implementation.

paper.title: Renewal Bias in Parallel Simulations of Absorbing Processes
paper.summary: Asynchronous parallel simulations of stochastic processes with absorbing states can exhibit systematic sampling bias when trajectory durations depend on their eventual absorbing outcomes. Workers that continuously restart upon absorption preferentially record rapidly terminating trajectories within a fixed computational budget, distorting the observed ensemble statistics. We investigate this effect using a minimal renewal model with two absorbing states and state-dependent exponential durations. Renewal theory yields exact expressions for the expected number and composition of completed trajectories, showing that the resulting bias decreases algebraically with execution time but persists as the number of parallel workers increases at fixed budget. We compare continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, which retains only the initial trajectory attempted by each worker. Although finite execution deadlines introduce residual censoring bias, this bias decreases exponentially with the computational budget. An analytical mean-squared error calculation reveals budget-dependent crossover worker allocations beyond which First-Trajectory Filtering becomes more accurate despite collecting fewer trajectories. We also examine the limitations of statistical inference under severe censoring when the absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown. Finally, simulations of the Axelrod model near its nonequilibrium transition demonstrate the preferential sampling of rapidly absorbing fragmented configurations, illustrating the relevance of the renewal mechanism in a spatially interacting system. Our results show that increasing computational throughput does not necessarily improve statistical accuracy and highlight the importance of accounting for trajectory-duration heterogeneity in parallel simulations of absorbing processes.

paper.title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow
paper.summary: Modons, or dipolar vortices, are a form of propagating vortex solution consisting of two counterrotating regions of fluid and moving together under self-advection. They are common features of the upper ocean that can remain stable over long times, thereby transporting fluid over large distances. Here, we present a semi-analytical method for finding modon solutions in a vertically-sheared background flow using the multi-layer quasi-geostrophic framework. This method works for arbitrarily many fluid layers and builds on our previous studies of multi-layer modon solutions. We present three example of modons in a background flow, highlighting the effect of varying relative potential velocity between layers and the impact of depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.

paper.title: Frequency-selective membrane-based metamaterial filters for low-insertion-loss harmonic crosstalk suppression in sub-harmonic THz receivers
paper.summary: Parasitic reflections and standing waves fundamentally limit amplitude stability and phase fidelity in coherent continuous-wave (CW) terahertz (THz) systems. We report a complementary metamaterial filter pair designed for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz in sub-harmonic heterodyne architectures. Fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes, the filters provide more than 30 dB stopband isolation while maintaining insertion losses below 1 dB in the passband. System-level coherent-imaging experiments demonstrate effective suppression of spurious-reflection-induced interference effects and improved spectral baseline stability. The filters mitigate wavefront distortions resulting from such interferences and enhance reconstruction robustness. These results establish membrane-based metamaterial filters as compact frequency-selective isolation elements for sub-harmonic heterodyne THz detection and highlight their potential for phase-engineered imaging and sensing applications.

paper.title: A Hierarchy of Fast and Strong Signatures for Vertex Orbits
paper.summary: The defining features of a physical system are its symmetries and its invariants. For a network, the symmetries are the automorphisms, and the invariants are the vertex orbits they define. Two vertices of a graph may appear structurally indistinguishable without being interchangeable under any graph automorphism. Distinguishing apparent similarity from genuine symmetry lies at the heart of the vertex-orbit partition problem. In this work, we develop a hierarchy of increasingly expressive, automorphism-invariant signatures that draw on the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the Dirac operator to reveal subtle structural differences. Guided by a sequence of counterexamples, we progressively strengthen these signatures, ultimately incorporating probing techniques, which are temporary structural perturbations, that expose the hidden distinctions in the original unperturbed graph. We evaluate our approach across diverse benchmark families, recovering exact orbit partitions in challenging instances, including graphs that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler--Leman refinement. We also examine the computational and numerical limitations of our constructions, distinguishing empirical success from theoretical completeness. Our findings highlight the potential of spectral and probing-based methods for uncovering the structural distinctions that define vertex orbit.

paper.title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
paper.summary: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

paper.title: Non-Equilibrium Ising-Bloch Transition in Polarization Cavity Solitons
paper.summary: Polarization cavity solitons in coherently driven Kerr resonators undergo a sequence of dynamical bifurcations as the cavity detuning is increased. Here we show that a stationary localized state containing an Ising wall first becomes a fixed breather and then develops finite chirality and drift motion through a spontaneous non-equilibrium Ising-Bloch transition. Stability analyses identify the modes responsible for the breathing and the motion, revealing controllable dynamics of polarization cavity solitons.

paper.title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
paper.summary: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

paper.title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality
paper.summary: Variational principles for dissipative processes come in two families: minimum principles at nonequilibrium stationary states (Helmholtz, Kirchhoff, Prigogine) and maximum principles for relaxation in continuum mechanics (Ziegler, Hackl, Fischer). We contribute to the understanding of the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) by investigating its extremal properties, and uncover the connection between the two families, whose distinction was recently made precise for diffusion: the extremal character is decided by the regime, which is either relaxation at frozen state, as in a closed system (maximum dissipation), or a driven stationary state in an open system (minimum dissipation), while the underlying Rayleighian functional is convex and minimized in both cases. We further examine the Reynolds transport theorem, a useful tool for fixing the energy rates of continua, and the role of inertia, recently argued to lie beyond the reach of Rayleighian principles. With inertia the driving force must be held fixed during the variation, which is less elegant than in the inertialess case, where it is a state function. Writing the energy rate as rates times driving forces still yields the correct equations, and an extremal statement survives whenever the frozen force does not depend on the varied rate. This holds directly for unsteady Stokes flow, and for Navier-Stokes flow after a change to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state and the convective term, nonvariational in the Eulerian description, does not appear. The framework is tested on the Navier-Stokes family (Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier-Stokes flow, in order of increasing complexity) and on dissipative Lagrangian mechanics.

paper.title: Boosting bottom-up milling of glass with GHz laser bursts
paper.summary: Burst-mode laser processing has gained increasing attention in material machining due to its potential to enhance processing efficiency and quality. However, most studies have focused on conventional top-down machining strategies, while investigations of bottom-up milling (BUM) remain limited. In this work, we optimize processing parameters for high-efficiency glass milling using a bottom-up approach with GHz bursts. The results show that the highest BUM efficiencies are achieved when employing high pulse counts ($\geq$ 20). To the best of our knowledge, we report the highest glass milling efficiency, reaching more than 250 $μ$m$^3$/$μ$J for both soda-lime glass and fused silica. Furthermore, increasing the burst repetition rate while maintaining a parameter set associated with high milling efficiency enables a material removal rate larger than 8 mm$^3$/s.

paper.title: Experimental Evidence of Cellular Sparing under Single-Pulse Picosecond Irradiation at Extreme Dose Rates
paper.summary: Understanding how biological cells respond to radiation delivered on extremely short timescales is central to resolving the fundamental mechanisms underlying radiotherapy and to defining new regimes of radiobiology. Experimentally accessing these earliest stages of physicochemical response is crucial to benchmark current numerical codes, whose predictions are known to vary substantially with under-constrained early-stage parameters. Using a laser-driven electron source, tunable doses up to 8Gy were delivered to normal and cancer human cell lines, in single pulses of picosecond-scale duration at mean dose rates above 10^10 Gy/s.
