paper.summary: Generation and evolution of turbulence at shock fronts are crucial aspects of the process of particle acceleration in different classes of sources. Here we aim at describing the fate of non-thermal particles and turbulence in the downstream region of an astrophysical shock, both in the case in which turbulence is solely produced upstream and advected through the shock and in the case in which additional turbulence is injected downstream. In particular we will provide an estimate of the effect of stochastic acceleration on particles accelerated at the shock and then advected behind it. The calculations will be specialized to supernova remnant shocks. The temporal evolution of the particle distribution function downstream of the shock and the power spectrum of the turbulent perturbations are both followed by solving numerically the transport equations for the two quantities, accounting for the damping of waves due to the particles that resonantly interact with them, which makes the problem non-linear. Our calculations show that, if waves are only self-generated upstream via Bell instability, they are not able to significantly modify the particle spectrum in the downstream region. Additionally, turbulent cascading in $k$-space quickly drains their energy, further limiting the stochastic acceleration of particles. If, on the other hand, there are additional sources of turbulence downstream, then these waves can contribute meaningfully to second order Fermi acceleration and alter the spectrum of particles. This may reflect in the spectrum of gamma radiation produced through $pp$ scattering downstream. Although second order Fermi acceleration is typically slower than diffusive shock acceleration, particles are expected to stay downstream of shocks for much longer times during which stochastic acceleration can modify their spectrum and affect the spectra of multi-messenger emissions.

paper.title: Dynamics of squeezed-state preparation in quadratic and Kerr nonlinear microresonators
paper.summary: We develop a dynamical model of squeezed-state generation in nonlinear optical microresonators that takes into account the back-action of the signal mode on the pump mode. The resonator is treated as an open quantum system, while the pump modes are described by time-dependent classical amplitudes, which allows pump depletion to be included beyond the standard undepleted-pump approximation. For a $χ^{(2)}$ microresonator, the model reproduces the conventional 3~dB intracavity squeezing limit below threshold and predicts a transient above-threshold regime in which this limit can be overcome for a finite time before pump depletion becomes appreciable. The dynamical approach is extended to a three-mode Kerr microresonator with two pump modes. Separately, we investigate stationary squeezing in a reduced five-mode model with fixed pump amplitudes, including a parasitic single-pump spontaneous four-wave-mixing channel. Within this model, the parasitic channel reduces the achievable squeezing and shifts the instability threshold to lower pump amplitudes. These results provide a compact framework for estimating the validity range of the undepleted-pump approximation and for analyzing transient squeezing dynamics in nonlinear microresonators.

paper.title: Wideband AR-HCF Transmission Under Variable Network Traffic: A System-Level Analysis
paper.summary: Dynamic traffic changes spectral occupancy in wideband optical links, perturbing surviving channels in single-mode fiber (SMF) through nonlinear interference (NLI), inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering, and amplifier loading. This motivates amplified-spontaneous-emission (ASE) idlers to maintain full occupancy. We test whether spectral filling remains necessary in antiresonant hollow-core fiber (AR-HCF) using a span-by-span model of a 96-channel, 9.6-THz extended-C+L link over 960 km. The model jointly tracks signal, ASE, and NLI, including amplifier pigtails, line-resolved CO2 absorption, intermodal interference, amplifier control, and load transients. At equal launch power, reducing occupancy from 100% to 20% changes surviving-channel generalized signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR) by just 0.0016 dB in AR-HCF versus 1.52 dB in SMF. At the AR-HCF throughput-optimal launch of +12.3 dBm/channel, the GSNR shift rises to 0.24 dB, nearly all from NLI in short solid-glass amplifier pigtails, chiefly the output pigtail. These pigtails hold the optimum 8.9 dB below the amplifier ceiling, but removing them yields only about 1% more throughput at that launch due to transceiver, intermodal-interference, and gas-absorption limits. Line-resolved gas modeling distinguishes several decibels of CO2 attenuation, largely offset by per-span equalization, from narrow absorption notches not recoverable by flat gain. Constant-gain control permits a 23% amplifier energy saving by tracking load, whereas constant-output control saves none. An 85% channel drop causes an 8.8-dB uncontrolled gain excursion, reduced to 0.6 dB with an assumed 500-Hz loop. Thus, AR-HCF shifts the constraints on elastic wideband transmission from fiber nonlinearities to amplifier-site components, gas absorption, and control dynamics.

paper.title: Dynamic Molecular Transformation Mediated Crystallization Regulation and Interface Passivation in Tin Based Perovskite Solar Cells
paper.summary: Tin-based perovskites are promising candidates for lead-free photovoltaics but suffer from labile Sn$^{2+}$ coordination, rapid crystallization, and severe interfacial defects. Here, we develop a dynamic molecular transformation using 1-acetylpiperazine (PX) to regulate crystallization and interface chemistry simultaneously. During nucleation and growth, the carbonyl group coordinates with Sn$^{2+}$ to stabilize precursor complexes, moderate supersaturation, and enable controlled crystal growth. Upon annealing, PX undergoes in situ molecular transformation, suggested to form amidinium-functionalized species that preferentially occupy surface A-site vacancies, forming a passivation layer and suppressing nonradiative recombination. This coupled bulk-to-interface evolution yields compact, highly crystalline films with improved optoelectronic quality. Devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 15.18% and retain 94.1% of initial efficiency after 500 h of continuous illumination. This work demonstrates a dynamic molecular engineering approach integrating crystallization control and interface passivation, providing a pathway toward efficient and stable lead-free perovskite photovoltaics.

paper.title: Intensity limits for phase-only holographic optical-tweezer arrays
paper.summary: Optical tweezers use tightly focused laser beams to trap and manipulate individual particles, enabling advances in quantum computing, drug discovery, and biological research. Scaling these technologies to large arrays requires delivering sufficient light to every trapping site while minimizing the total laser power required. Here, we investigate the fundamental limits of how efficiently a phase-only hologram can distribute light across an array of optical traps. We derive upper bounds on the minimum intensity across trapping sites, accounting for illumination, target geometry, and diffraction from spatial light modulator pixels. For arrays arranged in a single plane or across two axial planes, we show how these limits scale with the number of traps and SLM pixels, and establish conditions for focusing light in three dimensions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that optimized holograms can closely approach these theoretical limits, suggesting that further improvements in phase optimization alone offer limited power savings. Instead, our results reveal how the choice of illumination and trap geometry can improve light efficiency, providing practical guidelines for designing larger, more power-efficient optical-tweezer arrays.

paper.title: Adaptive wavefront shaping through flexible multicore photonic lantern fibres
paper.summary: Holographic micro-endoscopy enables images to be funnelled all-optically through hair-thin strands of optical fibre. Future applications of this technology encompass biomedical imaging within mobile organisms, LiDAR, and industrial inspection. Yet holographic imaging through dynamically flexible optical fibres, called for in many real-world scenarios, represents an ongoing challenge. In this work we demonstrate how a bespoke fibre architecture that we term a 'photonic lantern fibre' offers a way forward. This device benefits from the negligible modal cross-talk of a polarisation-maintaining multicore fibre throughout the majority of its length. A tapered region at one end - known as a photonic lantern - guides light to a short segment of multimode optical fibre. We show how this fibre enables the projection of high-fidelity structured light to the multimode distal fibre facet via wavefront shaping, providing a level of optical control beyond that possible using conventional multicore fibres which suffer from aliasing due to their spatially separated cores. Furthermore, we demonstrate how high-contrast distal focussing can be re-established, anywhere across the output facet, after the multicore fibre is arbitrarily contorted, without access to the distal end. To achieve this we introduce two in-situ bend compensation strategies, that rely on a distally mounted guide-star or analysis of light reflected from the distal facet - offering the future potential for rapid single-shot bend calibration. Our work paves a new route towards the controlled delivery of high-dimensional structured light fields through dynamically flexible optical fibres.

paper.title: How light interacts with matter, revisited
paper.summary: In 1968 Victor Weisskopf explained in Scientific American how light interacts with matter, with a few formulas and many words. We tell the same story again with the tools that have since become available: the fields are computed and drawn, and their evolution in time is shown in animations. Light is described as a classical electromagnetic field and matter as a collection of charged oscillators; every phenomenon follows from adding up the retarded waves radiated by the oscillators, each with its proper delay and phase. From this single picture we obtain the blue of the sky and the white of the clouds, transparency and the refractive index, the Ewald-Oseen extinction theorem, reflection and the colours of thin films, why metals reflect and what gives metals and semiconductors their colours, polarizers, Brewster's angle and birefringence, the working of mirrors, lenses, microscopes and the eye, the propagation of a few-cycle pulse through a slab, Cherenkov radiation, amplification and second-harmonic generation. Feynman's arrows are made quantitative with the sheet method, and coupled-dipole simulations show the incident wave being cancelled and replaced inside the medium. The connection with quantum theory is discussed where the classical picture stops: the photon, spontaneous emission and the forbidden lines of the aurora, vision and photosynthesis, and the sum over paths. The text is addressed to undergraduate students and their teachers, and to any reader curious about the physics behind everyday optical phenomena; derivations are collected in separate panels, and the animations and the Python codes used for the figures and simulations are provided as ancillary files.

paper.title: Differentiable Inverse Rendering Recovers Intrinsic Properties from Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography
paper.summary: Medical images encode intrinsic tissue properties that indicate disease progression, yet these properties remain entangled with the system-dependent physics of image formation. Differentiable inverse rendering asks whether they are recoverable by inverting the imaging system's forward physics rather than through post-hoc correction. We address this in optical coherence tomography (OCT), focusing on the optical attenuation coefficient, a per-pixel marker of pathology and cellular composition. Conventional recovery relies on closed-form inversions limited to simplified light-tissue models, or learned methods coupled to specific imaging configurations. We instead recover per-pixel attenuation from a single OCT image by gradient descent through a differentiable physics-based forward model. We verified the method against analytical solutions, validated it on five in vitro phantoms, and applied it without modification to 29{,}269 clinical intravascular OCT images from 128 patients. The inversion needs no training data or segmentations and is portable across platforms and retrospective archives. Replacing the forward model or recovering another optical parameter leaves the optimization procedure unchanged. We demonstrate per-pixel recovery is tractable because gradient information scales to this high-dimensional problem, where gradient-free methods become intractable. Our work supports quantitative tissue characterization from OCT images and provides a framework for extension across imaging modalities and organ systems.

paper.title: More particles or the pair? An exact test of how to improve mode-coupling theory
paper.summary: How a dense liquid arrests into a glass remains a central problem in physics. Mode-coupling theory (MCT), the leading microscopic theory of the glass transition, fails to reproduce mean-field caging. Two routes are proposed to repair it: tracking more-particle correlations, or enforcing repulsion within each colliding pair. Testing both on an exact benchmark liquid, we show that MCT lets touching spheres pass through each other at all orders: adding particles dilutes memory and worsens the transition, whereas restoring pair impenetrability recovers mean-field arrest and the cage size.

paper.title: A Microscopic Model Underpinning Macroscopic QED in Active Media
paper.summary: We establish a microscopic foundation for macroscopic quantum electrodynamics in active media. Starting from a driven three-level system, we derive an effective two-level description with nonequilibrium stationary populations and employ a quantum central limit approach to obtain collective Langevin dynamics. This construction yields the electromagnetic susceptibility and quantum noise-current correlations from the same microscopic stationary state, providing a direct connection to the reservoir operators of conventional macroscopic quantum electrodynamics. We show that the optical response is governed by the population difference, whereas the noise correlations depend separately on the populations of the two levels. Consequently, at optical transparency, the imaginary part of the susceptibility vanishes while quantum fluctuations remain finite. We interpret the resulting noise statistics in terms of an effective reservoir occupation and a purification involving two vacuum modes, and establish a corresponding effective-temperature fluctuation--dissipation relation. Finally, we demonstrate that the residual fluctuations at transparency can induce finite heating of a nearby quantum probe.

paper.title: Foreshortening of Polarizer Angles in Wide Field Polarizing Imagers
paper.summary: The Polarimeter to Unify Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) is a very wide field polarizing imager covering a 90 degree diameter region of the sky, stitched together from four individual fields of view (FOVs), three of which are supported by Wide Field Imagers (WFIs) with 40 degree diameter individual FOVs. The science objective requires precise measurement of linear polarization. The WFI FOV is sufficiently wide that polarizer angles are foreshortened by projection effects relative to the line of sight of each pixel in the instrument, deviating from their nominal angular positions of -60, 0, and +60 degree relative to the instrument frame of reference. These angles are foreshortened by the very wide WFI field of view, changing their effective angle across the image plane - an effect that is analogous to similar challenges of polarimetric right/left channel separation in large-format 3D cinema, such as the IMAX format. Using a simple geometrical approach we estimated the perceived polarizer angle in the WFI FOV will vary by +/-2.5 degree for +/-60 degree and +/-3.5 degree for 0 degree polarizer angles. We present the effect of this deviation on the polarized brightness to be recorded by WFI, along with how optical distortion will shift the location of foreshortened angles. We also discuss the implications of this effect on upcoming technologies based on polarimetry across in wide fields.

paper.title: Standoff chemical identification of harmful aerosols
paper.summary: Aerosols - solid or liquid particles suspended in air - are an effective means of dispersing chemical warfare agents and toxic pharmaceuticals, posing acute risks to public safety and security. Exposure to aerosol particulate matter in the environment and in industrial settings has also been linked to respiratory and cardiovascular disease. In both cases, rapid chemical identification is key to generating early warnings and attributing sources. Established methods chemically identify aerosols only after extracting a sample, while standoff techniques such as lidar classify aerosols only into broad categories. Chemical identification at a distance is hindered by aerosol extinction signatures that are weak, spectrally broad, and obscured by far stronger absorption from ambient gases. Here, we demonstrate time-resolved, standoff chemical differentiation of aerosols with dual-comb spectroscopy and machine learning identification algorithms. The high spectral resolution of dual-comb spectroscopy allows ambient gas absorption to be removed, and the algorithms identify chemicals without knowledge of aerosol size and morphology. We demonstrate identification of aerosolized benzyl fentanyl (a fentanyl simulant) in mixtures with other aerosols in a standoff measurement through ambient H2O, CO2, and CH4. Despite the aerosol producing only subtle, <1% changes in the extinction spectrum across hundreds of wavenumbers, we find the limit of identification to be an order of magnitude below lethal concentrations for a 1 m aerosol cloud. This technique provides a new paradigm for performing rapid chemical speciation of aerosols using their infrared absorption signatures without extractive sampling. Together with advances in chip-based mid-infrared dual-comb spectrometry, we anticipate this technique will enable real-time networks for standoff detection of aerosol emissions and aerosolized chemical threats.
